name: Adoption Rate
alsoknownas: % Adoption of Standards; % Adoption to Golden Standards
description: Relates to engineers’ uptake and sustained use of internal tools, workflows, and platforms, reflecting how effectively these resources integrate into daily workflows and solve critical problems. It serves as a key metric for assessing DevEx success and alignment with productivity goals.

implementation.cadence: Monthly, for the first two quarters after a tool or platform launches
implementation.target_goal: 70% or more of the eligible population active in a given week, within 90 days of launch
telemetry_sources: Okta or Entra ID sign-in logs
recipe_steps: Define the eligible population explicitly: which teams or roles are actually expected to use this tool. Adoption against the whole company is misleading.
Pull weekly active users from the tool's own admin analytics, or from SSO sign-in logs where the tool has no reporting of its own.
Divide active users by the eligible population, and report weekly active rather than any-time-used.
Segment by team to find where adoption has stalled rather than treating the organisation as one number.
Talk to two or three non-adopting teams each month. The reason for non-adoption is the actionable part, not the percentage.

name: Application Startup Duration
description: The time needed to startup an application locally.

implementation.cadence: Weekly, from an automated benchmark run
implementation.target_goal: Median cold start under 30 seconds on a reference developer machine
telemetry_sources: Vite or Webpack dev server logs
Custom timing wrapper in the start script
recipe_steps: Define cold start and warm start separately and measure only one of them. Mixing the two produces a number nobody can act on.
Wrap the local start command in a timing script that logs duration, environment and machine type to a shared location.
Collect from developer machines over a week, or run a scheduled benchmark on reference hardware if collection from laptops is too intrusive.
Report the median and the 85th percentile. Startup time is heavily affected by caches and hardware, so the spread matters more than the average.
Record the hardware profile alongside the figure. A change in the fleet will move this metric without anything in the codebase changing.

name: Branch Lifetime
description: The time elapsed between branch creation until merge to main/production.

implementation.target_goal: Median under 2 days; no active branch older than 5 days
recipe_steps: Extract branch creation and merge timestamps from the VCS API, or from git reflog where the API does not expose creation time.
Exclude long-lived release, integration and vendor branches, which are intentionally long and will distort the median.
Report the median lifetime alongside a count of branches currently open for more than 5 days. The count is the more actionable of the two.
Review the oldest open branches with the team each week and decide explicitly whether to merge, split or close each one.
Treat a rising median as a signal about change size and review latency rather than about individual developers.

name: Burnout Risk Score
description: Evaluates developers’ mental health, job fulfillment, and workplace conditions. It serves as a critical indicator of systemic issues that harm productivity and retention.

implementation.target_goal: No team scoring in the at-risk band; treat any movement as a trigger for a conversation, never as a performance target
recipe_steps: Use an established short workplace wellbeing scale rather than inventing questions. Workload, recovery, autonomy and support are the usual dimensions.
Run it anonymously and report only at team level, with a minimum of five responses per team, so no individual can be identified from the aggregate.
State in writing before the first run that scores will never be used in performance review, promotion or individual feedback. Without that commitment the responses will not be honest.
Read the score alongside objective workload signals such as after-hours commit activity, on-call frequency and unplanned work share.

Agree in advance who acts on a poor result and what they are empowered to change. This is an indicator of working conditions, not a clinical assessment, and the action belongs with whoever controls workload and staffing.

name: Business Objective Advancement
description: Refers to measuring how effectively software development efforts align with and contribute to achieving specific organizational goals. This metric focuses on outcome-driven impact rather than raw activity metrics (e.g., lines of code, commits).

implementation.cadence: Quarterly, reviewed with product and business stakeholders
implementation.target_goal: 70% or more of completed engineering work traceable to a stated objective; set the threshold locally in the first quarter
telemetry_sources: Jira with epic to OKR links
recipe_steps: Require every epic or initiative to carry a link to a stated company or product objective. Without that link at the point of planning, nothing can be traced afterwards.
Measure the share of completed work that carries such a link, and track unlinked work separately rather than discarding it.
Report the distribution of effort across objectives, not a claim of value delivered. This metric shows where effort went, which is alignment, not impact.
Review the distribution with product each quarter and ask whether it matches stated priorities. The mismatch is the finding, not the percentage itself.
State the limitation explicitly when reporting: causally linking engineering work to business outcomes remains unsolved, and this metric deliberately does not attempt it.

name: Change Failure Rate
alsoknownas: Change Fail Percentage; Change Fail Rate
description: This metric measures the percentage of deployments that cause failures in production, requiring hotfixes or rollbacks. A lower change failure rate indicates a more reliable delivery process.

implementation.cadence: Weekly, reported as a rolling 4-week average
implementation.target_goal: Under 15% of production deployments require a hotfix or rollback
recipe_steps: Agree a written definition of a failed change with the team: a deployment that triggers a rollback, a hotfix within 24 hours, or a Sev1/Sev2 incident.
Tag each production deployment in your CI/CD tool or deployment log so deployments can be counted reliably.
Link incidents and hotfix PRs back to the deployment that caused them, by release tag or commit SHA.
Divide failed deployments by total deployments for the period and track the rolling 4-week average rather than single weeks.
Review spikes in the retro and look for a cause in test coverage, deployment size or review depth before setting a target.

name: CI Determinism
description: The opposite of test flakiness: the chance that a test suite’s result will be valid (not a flake) ensures that identical inputs in a continuous integration (CI) pipeline always produce the same outputs (binaries, artifacts, test results). This guarantees reproducibility, reliability, and traceability in software builds, critical for debugging, compliance, and safety-critical systems.

implementation.target_goal: 99% or more of test runs deterministic, i.e. a flake rate under 1%
recipe_steps: Detect flakes automatically by re-running failed tests against the same commit. A test that passes on retry without a code change is flaky by definition.
Record each flaky occurrence against the test name so repeat offenders are visible, rather than only counting failures in aggregate.
Calculate determinism as one minus flaky runs divided by total runs, and report it weekly alongside the count of distinct flaky tests.
Quarantine the worst offenders so they stop blocking merges, but cap how long a test may stay quarantined. An unbounded quarantine list becomes permanent.
Fix or delete quarantined tests rather than relying on automatic retries. Retries hide the problem and slowly increase pipeline time.

name: CI Pipeline Failure Rate
description: Measures the percentage of builds or automated workflows in a continuous integration (CI) system that fail due to errors (e.g., compilation issues, test failures, dependency conflicts).

implementation.target_goal: Under 15% of runs failing overall, and under 2% failing for infrastructure reasons
recipe_steps: Export run outcomes from the CI provider's API rather than counting red badges by hand.
Classify each failure by cause: test failure, compilation error, infrastructure or timeout, and dependency resolution. A single blended percentage is not actionable.
Report the breakdown by cause, not the headline rate. A pipeline failing because tests catch real bugs is working correctly.
Treat infrastructure and dependency failures as the actionable subset and set a separate, much tighter target for them.
Review the most frequent single cause each week. Pipeline failures cluster heavily, so one fix usually removes most of the noise.

name: CI Build Time
alsoknownas: CI Pipeline P50 Build Time; Post-Commit CI Speed
description: Refers to the (median or mean) duration of successful builds in a continuous integration (CI) pipeline. Might be quantified for individual or a group of commits.

implementation.target_goal: Median under 10 minutes for successful builds
recipe_steps: Measure successful builds only. Failed builds exit early and will flatter the median if included.
Pull duration per run from the CI provider's API and report the median with the 85th percentile beside it.
Break the total down by pipeline stage: checkout, dependency install, compile, test, package. The distribution matters more than the total.
Attack the single longest stage first, usually through caching, parallelism or test splitting, and re-measure before moving to the next.
Watch for slow growth over months rather than week-to-week noise. Build time creeps up a few seconds at a time and is rarely noticed until it hurts.

name: Code Churn
description: Is the amount of code rewritten shortly after being written.

implementation.target_goal: No fixed target. Investigate when churn exceeds roughly 25% of lines changed in a period
recipe_steps: Define churn precisely before measuring: lines written and then changed again within a fixed window, typically 21 or 30 days. Note that this differs from Code Rework Rate, which counts how often changes touch recent code rather than how much code is rewritten.
Compute it from git history by comparing line authorship dates against subsequent modifications, excluding generated files, vendored dependencies and bulk reformatting.
Aggregate at repository or team level only. Churn attributed to individuals is misleading and punishes the people doing exploratory work.
Read a spike as a signal about unclear requirements or a difficult area of the codebase, not about developer quality.
Compare churn across areas of the codebase rather than over time. The hotspots are where the finding usually is.

name: Code Reviewer Response Time
alsoknownas: Code Reviewer Response Time (P50 and P90); Diff Response Time
description: Measures how long it takes, in business hours, for code reviewers to respond to each update of the code review from the author.

implementation.target_goal: Median first response under 4 business hours
recipe_steps: Measure time to the first substantive human response, not the first comment. Bot and linter comments will otherwise make this metric look excellent while reviewers are absent.
Count business hours rather than wall clock, and handle time zones explicitly if the team is distributed. A pull request opened on Friday evening should not register as a 60-hour wait.
Report the median and the 85th percentile. The tail is where the frustration lives and the median will hide it.
Segment by pull request size. Large changes legitimately wait longer, and mixing them with one-line fixes obscures both.
Act with a review rota or an explicit team agreement on response time rather than by reporting the number. Visibility alone rarely changes reviewer behaviour.

name: Code Rework Rate
alsoknownas: PR revert rate
description: Is the percentage of code changes that modify recently changed code.

implementation.target_goal: Under 15% of changes modifying code less than 30 days old
recipe_steps: Define recent explicitly, typically code written within the last 30 days. Note that this differs from Code Churn, which measures the volume of rewritten lines rather than how frequently changes touch recent code.
For each commit, use git blame to establish the age of the lines it modifies, and mark the commit as rework if a meaningful share of those lines are recent.
Exclude planned refactors and migrations, which are intentional rework and will distort the rate if counted.
Report at team and codebase-area level. Rework concentrates in specific modules, and naming the module is the actionable output.
Read it next to Code Churn. Together they distinguish a lot of rewriting in one place from frequent small revisits across the codebase, which have different causes.

name: Produced Code
alsoknownas: Code Owned by Time; Commit Count; Committed Source Lines of Code by Time; Engineering Productivity; KLOC - Lines of Code; Lines Deleted; Lines Inserted; Number of Lines of Code Modified; Source Lines of Code by Time
description: Tracks contributions to the codebase, for example by number of lines of code.

implementation.target_goal: No target. This is a diagnostic signal, never a goal
recipe_steps: xtract added and deleted lines per repository with git log --numstat over the reporting period.
Exclude generated code, vendored dependencies, lockfiles and bulk reformatting commits, or the figure will be dominated by noise.
Aggregate at repository or team level only. Lines of code per developer is a well-documented anti-pattern and invites gaming.
Use the figure solely as context for other metrics, for example explaining a change in review load or cycle time.
Set no target and do not report it to leadership in isolation.

name: Cognitive Load Score
alsoknownas: Cognitive Effort
description: Self-reported mental effort required to perform tasks. Avoiding multitasking, high WIP (work in progress) counts, and attention splitting to maintain focus and reduce cognitive overhead.

implementation.target_goal: Mean under 2.5 on a 5-point load scale, where lower is better
recipe_steps: Use an established instrument rather than inventing questions. The NASA-TLX short form, reduced to mental demand, effort and frustration, is well validated and takes under a minute to answer.
Anchor the question to a specific recent task rather than asking about work in general. Generalised answers drift towards mood and stop tracking anything measurable.
Run it on the same cadence every time, ideally attached to an existing ritual such as sprint close, so it does not feel like an extra demand.
Read the score alongside objective load signals you already have: work in progress count, number of concurrent assignments and context switches per day.
Act on the task types that score highest rather than on the overall average. Cognitive load is concentrated in particular kinds of work, and that is where tooling or documentation will help.

name: CI/CD Health Score
description: Measures the effectiveness of automated build, test, and deployment processes in enabling rapid, reliable software delivery.

implementation.target_goal: Set locally after a four-week baseline. There is no transferable target for a composite score
recipe_steps: Build the score from three or four component metrics you already collect, such as build time, pipeline failure rate, determinism and deployment frequency. Do not introduce new collection for a composite.
Normalise each component to a 0-100 scale against a locally agreed good and bad bound, and write those bounds down. An unexplained composite is impossible to act on.
State the weighting explicitly and keep it stable. A score whose weights change quietly cannot be compared across quarters.
Always display the component values next to the composite. The score is a conversation starter; the components are what anyone actually acts on.
Review after two quarters whether anyone drills into the components. If nobody does, retire the composite rather than maintaining a number that looks informative and changes nothing.

name: Contribution Volume
alsoknownas: Number of Modifications / Modules / WorkItems / Requirements
description: The number of contribution units, such as modifications, modules touched, work items closed, or requirements implemented, by an individual developer or team within a period. Used to spot trends in team capacity, not as a standalone productivity score.

implementation.target_goal: No target. Use for capacity trends only, never as a productivity score
recipe_steps: Pick one contribution unit and keep it fixed: work items closed, modules touched or requirements implemented. Switching units breaks the trend.
Aggregate at team level. The metric's own definition warns against standalone use, and per-developer reporting converts it into a target that will be met by splitting work.
Annotate the series with leave, onboarding, incidents and holidays before anyone reads it. Most apparent changes in volume have a mundane explanation.
Use it for capacity planning and for spotting sustained shifts, not for comparing teams against each other. Different teams work on different kinds of problems.
Pair it with an outcome or quality metric whenever it is reported, so rising volume at falling quality is visible in the same view.

name: Cost Savings
description: Relates to strategic reductions in product development and operational expenses achieved through optimized engineering practices, aligning technical efficiency with business profitability. This is measured by tracking how engineering improvements directly lower costs while maintaining quality and delivery speed.

implementation.target_goal: Set per initiative when it is proposed. An organisation-wide target is not meaningful for this metric
recipe_steps: Measure per initiative, never in aggregate. A single savings figure for the organisation cannot be traced to any decision and will not survive scrutiny.
Record the baseline cost before the change, over a window long enough to cover normal variation, and agree that window with finance in advance.
Separate hard savings, where an invoice actually falls, from avoided cost, which is an estimate of spend that did not happen. Report them as two numbers and never merge them.
Write down the counterfactual assumption: what would have happened without this work. Most disputed savings claims fail at this step rather than at the arithmetic.
Have finance confirm the figure before it is reported outside engineering. An unverified savings claim damages credibility more than having no number at all.

name: Customer Satisfaction Score
alsoknownas: CSAT; Customer Experience; Customer Satisfaction; Customer Satisfaction Scores; NPS; User/customer satisfaction
description: Measures how pleased customers are with a product, service, or interaction, typically via surveys. Responses are aggregated into a percentage score representing the proportion of satisfied customers

implementation.cadence: Quarterly for relational surveys, or continuously after support interactions
implementation.target_goal: 80% or more of respondents satisfied, meaning 4 or 5 on a 5-point scale
recipe_steps: Decide whether you are measuring transactional satisfaction, asked right after an interaction, or relational satisfaction, asked periodically about the product overall. Do not mix the two in one score.
Keep it to one rating question plus one open text question. Longer surveys lower the response rate, and the response rate is what determines whether the score means anything.
Report the response rate next to the score every time. A 90% satisfaction score from 11 responses is not a finding.
Segment by customer type or plan. An average across very different customers hides the group whose experience is actually deteriorating.
Route the open text verbatims to the team that owns the relevant area. The free text is where the actionable content is; the number only tells you whether to look.

name: Number of Customer-Reported Defects
description: Bugs reported by customers in production.

implementation.target_goal: A declining trend once normalised by active users or releases; no absolute target
recipe_steps: Define customer-reported precisely and distinguish it from internally found defects. Tag the source at intake, because reconstructing it later is unreliable.
Normalise by active users or by number of releases. A growing product will report more defects without getting worse, and the raw count will be misread as regression.
Segment by severity and report the severity mix alongside the count. Ten cosmetic issues and one data-loss bug are not the same month.
Track time from release to first report as a secondary signal. Defects found quickly by customers point at gaps in test coverage rather than at code quality generally.
Review the top recurring defect area each month. Customer-reported defects cluster, and naming the component is the actionable output.

name: Cycle Time
alsoknownas: PR Cycle Time; Time From Creating a Patch to Patch Release; Time to Merge (TTM); Time to Value
description: Measures the time from code commit to code running in production. Shows how quickly team can respond to business needs.

implementation.target_goal: Median under 2 working days from first commit to production
recipe_steps: Fix the start and end points: first commit on the branch, and the deployment that carries that commit to production.
Extract both timestamps and join them on commit SHA present in the deployment metadata.
Report the median and the 85th percentile. The mean is distorted by a handful of long-running changes.
Break the total into coding, review wait, review and deploy wait, so the longest stage is visible.
Act on the longest stage only. Review wait is usually the largest and the cheapest to improve.

name: Number of Defects
alsoknownas: Defect Density; Defects per Function Point; Weighted Defects
description: Measures defect density: the number of errors or failures normalized by a size unit (e.g., function points), sometimes severity-weighted, indicating codebase quality independent of project size.

implementation.target_goal: A declining defect density against your chosen size unit; set the baseline in the first quarter
recipe_steps: Choose the size unit you will normalise by, such as function points, thousands of lines of code, or releases shipped. Every option is imperfect, so pick one, write down why, and keep it fixed.
Tag defects consistently at intake with component and severity. Retrospective tagging is unreliable and will quietly corrupt the series.
Decide whether to severity-weight the count. If you do, state the weights explicitly, because an unweighted and a weighted density are not comparable.
Report per component or service rather than for the whole codebase. Defects concentrate, and the aggregate hides where the problem is.
Do not compare density across projects that use different size units or different defect definitions. The comparison will be wrong in a way that is hard to see.

name: Deployment Frequency
description: How often an organization deploys code/builds to a production environment, regardless of whether that change is yet visible to end users. Higher deployment frequency indicates a more agile and responsive delivery process.

implementation.target_goal: At least one production deployment per service per week; daily or more for teams targeting the DORA elite band
recipe_steps: Write down what counts as a deployment: a change reaching the production environment, whether or not it is visible to users behind a flag.
Count deployment events from your CD pipeline rather than from release tickets, which are often created late or in batches.
Report per service as well as per team. A single team average hides one busy service carrying several dormant ones.
Track rollbacks separately so they do not inflate the count.
Compare against the published DORA bands to decide whether the current rate is worth acting on.

name: Deployment Success Rate
alsoknownas: Build Success Rate
description: The percentage of deployment (CI/CD) runs that complete successfully.

implementation.target_goal: 95% or more of deployment runs completing successfully
recipe_steps: Define success as the pipeline completing and the service passing its health check afterwards, not merely a green pipeline. A deploy that completes and leaves the service unhealthy is not a success.

Distinguish this from two neighbouring metrics before reporting it: Change Failure Rate counts deployments that succeed and then cause production incidents, and CI Pipeline Failure Rate covers build pipelines rather than deployments.
Exclude manually cancelled runs, which otherwise register as failures and make the rate look worse than it is.
Classify failures by cause: configuration, migration, timeout, dependency or health check. The cause breakdown is the actionable part.
Fix the single most frequent cause each month. Deployment failures cluster tightly around a small number of recurring problems.

name: Number of Deploys per Service
description: This metric in software engineering measures how often a specific service or microservice is deployed within a given timeframe. This metric is commonly used in DevOps and microservices architectures to track deployment frequency across different services.

implementation.target_goal: No service going a full month without a deployment
recipe_steps: Establish a service inventory first. You cannot measure deploys per service without an agreed list of services, and most teams discover the list is out of date.
Map each deployment to a service through the pipeline or repository, and record the mapping rather than inferring it each time.
Report the distribution across services, not the average. One frequently deployed service will hide a dozen dormant ones in any mean.
Treat this as distinct from Deployment Frequency, which measures the aggregate rate for a team or organisation. This metric exists to expose the spread between services.
Investigate services with no deploys for a month. Dormant services accumulate unpatched dependencies and undocumented drift, and the risk is invisible in aggregate figures.

name: Design
description: Captures documentation quality, architectural decisions, and prototyping efforts.

implementation.target_goal: Set locally when the metric is defined. The catalog definition is deliberately broad and has no transferable target
recipe_steps: Narrow the scope before measuring. This metric covers documentation quality, architectural decisions and prototyping, which are three different things with three different remedies. Pick one.
If you choose architectural decisions, adopt architecture decision records first. Without a standard place for decisions there is nothing to count.
Measure coverage rather than quality for the automated part, for example the share of significant changes that have a recorded decision. Quality needs human judgement and belongs in the survey.
Add one survey question for perceived quality, for example whether developers can understand why the current architecture is the way it is.
Revisit the definition each quarter. A broad metric that is never narrowed will produce a number nobody can act on.

name: Local Build Time
alsoknownas: Application/Package Build Duration; Build Time; Build Time Efficiency; Developer Build Time
description: Measures the time, in seconds, developers spend waiting for their builds to finish locally during development. Impacts developer flow and productivity. Considered e.g. as median (P50) or P90.

implementation.target_goal: Median under 2 minutes and P90 under 5 minutes for incremental builds
telemetry_sources: Custom shell wrapper around the build command
recipe_steps: Separate incremental builds from clean builds and measure them independently. Mixing them produces a bimodal distribution where neither the median nor the mean describes anything real.
Instrument the local build command to log duration, build type and machine profile to a shared location, rather than asking developers to report times.
Report P50 and P90 as the catalog definition suggests. The P90 is what breaks flow and is the number worth acting on.
Keep this distinct from CI Build Time, which runs on uniform hardware. Local build time varies with the developer's machine and the two cannot be compared directly.
Record the hardware profile alongside each measurement, so a change in the laptop fleet is not mistaken for a change in the build.

name: Developer Satisfaction
alsoknownas: AI tool CSAT; CSAT; DSAT; Developer Satisfaction; Developer Sentiment; Employee satisfaction; NSAT; Net User Satisfaction; Platform and Tool Satisfaction; Satisfaction Score; Satisfaction with Engineering System
description: Customer satisfaction score for developers. Measures developer and team happiness with regards to development systems.

implementation.target_goal: Net positive score >= 75% (or average rating >= 4.0 / 5.0)
recipe_steps: Deploy a 3-question pulse survey asking: ""How satisfied are you with our development tooling, workflows, and inner-loop speed?"" (1-5 scale).
Collect responses anonymously across a 5-day survey window to encourage candid feedback.
Calculate the percentage of positive respondents (rating 4 or 5) and segment results by squad to isolate tooling bottlenecks.
Review open-text blocker comments alongside score trends to prioritize platform improvements for the next cycle.

name: Velocity Index Benchmark
description: The Developer Velocity Index (DVI) is a survey that measures an enterprise’s technology, working practices, and organizational enablement and benchmarks them against peers. This comparison helps unearth specific areas of opportunity, whether in backlog management, testing, or security and compliance. For example, one company, well known for its technological progress and all-star developers, sought to define standard working practices more thoughtfully for cross-team collaboration after discovering a high amount of dissatisfaction, rework, and inefficiency reported by developers.

implementation.target_goal: Improvement against your own previous assessment. A peer-relative target requires a benchmark dataset most organisations do not have
recipe_steps: Be clear which instrument you are running. The Developer Velocity Index is a proprietary McKinsey assessment, and a self-built survey covering similar ground should not be called DVI.
If you build an internal adaptation, cover the same dimensions the original does: tooling, working practices, and organisational enablement such as culture and talent management.
Run it annually. These dimensions move slowly, and a quarterly cadence produces noise and survey fatigue without new information.
Benchmark against your own previous year unless you have access to a genuine peer dataset. Comparing against published industry figures from a different instrument is not a benchmark.
Use the result to identify two or three areas of opportunity and act on those. The value is in the dimension-level detail, not the headline index.

name: Diff Authoring Time
alsoknownas: Coding Time; Commits Performed by Time; Diff Authoring Time (DAT); Diffs per Engineer (PRs or MRs); Implementation Time per User Story; PR Authoring Time; Task Completion Time; Time Spent per Task; Time to Commit per LOC Changed
description: Aims to capture all active human developer time spent on a particular diff, split by the different roles involved. This information is made available in a privacy-aware manner. Active human work on a computer tends to be highly sequential, even if such individual sequences can be extremely short.

implementation.target_goal: Median under one working day from first commit to review-ready
recipe_steps: Approximate authoring time as first commit on the branch to the pull request leaving draft state. True active keyboard time needs IDE telemetry that most teams should not deploy.
Exclude branches that sit in draft for days without commits, which represent abandoned or parked work rather than slow authoring.
Report aggregates only, never per developer, and say so when publishing. This metric reads as surveillance if attributed individually.
Segment by change size, since a large refactor and a one-line fix are not comparable.
State the measurement limitation alongside the number so readers do not treat the proxy as exact.

name: Discoverability of Documentation and Expertise
description: Refers to how easily developers can locate critical information (e.g., codebase guides, API references) or identify colleagues with specific knowledge.

implementation.target_goal: 80% or more agreeing they can find what they need within 15 minutes
recipe_steps: Ask two separate questions: whether people can find the documentation they need, and whether they can identify the right colleague to ask. These fail for different reasons and need different fixes.
Anchor the question to a time, for example within 15 minutes. Without an anchor, answers drift towards whether the information exists at all rather than whether it was findable.
Pull failed and zero-result searches from your wiki's search analytics. That list is a direct inventory of missing or badly named documentation.
Count repeated questions in team channels as a supporting signal. A question asked three times in a quarter indicates documentation that exists but cannot be found, or does not exist.
Fix the top three gaps each quarter rather than trying to move the score. The score follows the gaps; the gaps do not follow the score.

name: Ease of Delivery
alsoknownas: Ease
description: Refers to how simple, straightforward, and frictionless it is for developers or teams to deliver software, features, or updates through their development processes and tooling. Captures the perceived and actual effort required to move work from development to production.

implementation.cadence: Quarterly, in the same week each quarter
implementation.target_goal: Mean of 4.0 or higher on a 5-point scale, or 75% agreement or better
recipe_steps: Ask one anchor question: ""How easy was it to deliver your work over the past quarter?"" on a 1 to 5 scale.
Follow it with one open text question: ""What slowed you down most?"" The free text is where the actionable content is.
Run it in the same week each quarter so the trend is comparable and the survey becomes predictable rather than disruptive.
Segment by team and tenure. New joiners and long-tenured developers routinely report very different experiences.
Read the score next to Cycle Time. Where perception and measured delivery speed disagree, the gap is the thing worth investigating.

name: Engineer Engagement
alsoknownas: Developer Engagement; Engagement
description: Refers to the emotional commitment, motivation, and involvement that software engineers or developers have toward their work, team, and organization.

implementation.cadence: Quarterly, aligned to any existing company engagement survey
implementation.target_goal: 75% or more favourable responses
recipe_steps: Check whether HR already runs an engagement survey and add engineering-specific items to it rather than launching a second one. Two overlapping surveys halve the response rate on both.

Keep this distinct from neighbouring metrics when you report it: Developer Satisfaction covers tooling and systems, Burnout Risk Score covers workload and conditions, and engagement covers commitment to the work, the team and the organisation.
Ask about motivation, belonging and belief in the direction of the work as separate items. A single engagement number cannot be acted on.
Segment by tenure. Engagement typically dips at particular points in the employment lifecycle, and the aggregate hides which cohort is affected.
Read it next to regrettable attrition. Engagement that falls two quarters before people leave is the signal worth having; engagement reported alone rarely changes anything.

name: Error Rates
alsoknownas: Defect Rate
description: Quantifies the frequency of user or system mistakes during interactions with a product (e.g., failed API requests, UI slips, or task errors)

implementation.target_goal: Under 1% of requests returning server errors; set separate thresholds per critical user flow
recipe_steps: Separate system errors from user errors before anything else. Server failures and users mistyping a form have different owners and different remedies, and blending them produces a number nobody acts on.
Set rates per endpoint or per critical user flow rather than one global figure. A global error rate is dominated by your highest-traffic endpoint and hides failures everywhere else.
Exclude known bot and scanner traffic, which can account for most 4xx responses and will swamp genuine user errors.
Alert on rate of change rather than on an absolute threshold. A doubling from 0.1% to 0.2% matters more than a steady 0.9%.
Attribute the top recurring errors to an owning team each week. Errors concentrate heavily, and naming the owner is what turns the number into action.

name: Experience of New Members
description: Is a combination of satisfaction, well-being and integration indicators to ensure new developers feel supported, included and able to contribute effectively.

implementation.cadence: At 30, 60 and 90 days after each new hire's start date
implementation.target_goal: 4.0 or higher on a 5-point scale at the 90-day mark, with every hire completing the 30-day check
telemetry_sources: Onboarding checklist in Notion or Confluence
recipe_steps: Trigger the survey from each hire's start date, not on a calendar quarter. Onboarding experience is relative to time in role, and a quarterly cadence will sample people at random points.
Ask about practical support, clarity of expectations and sense of belonging as separate items. They fail independently and have different fixes.
Keep the 30-day survey to three questions. New joiners are the least likely group to complete a long survey and the most valuable to hear from.
Pair it with an objective signal such as time to first merged pull request, so perceived and actual ramp-up can be compared.
Act within the cohort: feedback from the 30-day check should change the next hire's first month. Onboarding feedback that is only reviewed annually has no mechanism to improve anything.

name: Experiment Velocity
alsoknownas: A/B Test Throughput
description: Refers to the speed and efficiency at which the platform conducts and evaluates A/B tests to optimize features, algorithms, and user experiences.

implementation.target_goal: Median experiment reaching a decision within 3 weeks, with 80% or more of started experiments reaching a conclusion
recipe_steps: Define the clock explicitly: idea to live, or live to decision. These measure different bottlenecks and teams routinely report one while believing they measure the other.
Count experiments that reach a conclusion, not experiments started. Abandoned tests are the most common failure mode and counting starts will hide them.
Report the decision rate alongside the speed. An organisation running experiments quickly but concluding few of them has a worse problem than a slow one.
Require a pre-registered success metric and sample size before an experiment goes live, otherwise the decision step has nothing to decide against.

Check you have the traffic to support experimentation at all before adopting this metric. Below a few thousand weekly users per variant, most tests will never reach significance and the metric will measure patience rather than velocity.

name: Failed Deployment Recovery Time
description: This metric measures the time it takes to recover from a failed deployment (e.g. outage or service failure in production). A lower recovery time indicates a more resilient and responsive system.

implementation.target_goal: Median under 15 minutes from detection to service restored
recipe_steps: Define the clock as detection of the failed deployment to service restored, whether restoration came from a rollback or a fix forward.

Keep this distinct from Mean Time to Recover, which covers all incidents. This metric is specifically about deployments that fail, and the remedies are mostly in the deployment pipeline rather than in incident response.
Record which recovery path was used. Rollbacks and fix-forwards have very different durations, and a median that mixes them describes neither.
Automate rollback on health check failure where the deployment tool supports it. This is the single change that moves this metric most.
Rehearse a rollback deliberately each quarter. Teams routinely discover that the documented rollback path no longer works only during a real incident.

name: Feedback Latency
alsoknownas: CI Feedback Time; Time to Feedback
description: The average time between a developer action (e.g., code push, PR submission, build trigger) and the developer receiving a response (e.g., CI/test results, build status, review comments).

implementation.target_goal: Automated feedback under 10 minutes; human feedback under 4 business hours
recipe_steps: List the feedback loops you actually care about and measure each separately: local test run, CI result, review response, and deployment confirmation. A single blended latency figure is not interpretable.
Split automated from human feedback. They have completely different causes and completely different fixes, and averaging them hides both.

Note the overlap with neighbouring metrics: CI Build Time and Code Reviewer Response Time each measure one loop within this one. If you already track those, this metric adds value only by covering the loops they miss.
Report the slowest loop rather than the average. Developers experience the worst wait, not the mean one.
Use business hours for human loops and wall clock for automated ones. Mixing the two conventions makes the comparison between loops meaningless.

name: Focus Time
alsoknownas: Deep Work; Flow State; Focused Work; Uninterrupted Time
description: The ability to work in focus or flow, i.e. uninterrupted, in meeting-free blocks that allow the developer to concentrate deeply on their work. Often reported as percentage of total time or average time.

implementation.target_goal: At least two uninterrupted blocks of 2 hours or more per developer per day
recipe_steps: Define a focus block explicitly, for example 2 hours or more with no scheduled meeting, during working hours.
Pull calendar data through the Calendar or Graph API and compute blocks per developer per week.
Report team aggregates only. Per-developer calendar analysis is intrusive and will cost you the trust the metric depends on.
Add one self-report question each quarter asking whether people felt able to focus. Calendar data shows availability, not whether focus actually happened.
Act on meeting clustering rather than meeting count. Three meetings in a block leaves far more usable time than three meetings scattered across a day.

name: Impact
alsoknownas: Direct Customer Impact Measures
description: Evaluates the tangible outcomes and value delivered by development efforts. Unlike raw outputs (e.g., lines of code), impact focuses on business results and user-centric effects of software work. Making significant contributions to one’s business unit or area of ownership, ensuring that work has a tangible impact.

implementation.target_goal: Set locally per team. There is no transferable target, and a company-wide impact figure is not meaningful
telemetry_sources: Jira with an outcome field on epics
recipe_steps: Define impact in terms of each team's own area of ownership rather than through one company-wide formula. A platform team and a customer-facing team produce incomparable outcomes.

Require every completed initiative to record an observed outcome after the fact, not the projected outcome written when it was proposed. The gap between the two is the most useful thing this metric produces.
Accept qualitative evidence where numbers do not exist. A documented customer account of what changed is better data than a fabricated percentage.

Distinguish it from its neighbours when reporting: Business Objective Advancement measures whether work was aligned to objectives, and Initiative Progress and ROI measures financial return on DevEx investments. This metric asks whether the work mattered.

Review it in a forum with product and business stakeholders rather than putting it on a dashboard. Impact requires argument and context, and a number on a screen will be read as precision it does not have.

name: Initiative Progress and ROI
description: Measures the financial impact and advancement of specific developer experience (DevEx) improvement projects, linking technical efforts to business outcomes. It evaluates whether investments in tools, processes, or workflows deliver measurable returns.

implementation.target_goal: Payback within two quarters, agreed per initiative when it is proposed
telemetry_sources: The DevEx metric the initiative targets
recipe_steps: Name the specific DevEx metric each initiative is meant to move, and record its baseline before work starts. An initiative without a named target metric cannot have a return calculated afterwards.
Estimate cost as engineering time at a standard internal rate plus any licence or infrastructure spend. Keep the rate constant across initiatives so they remain comparable.
Re-measure the target metric after an agreed period, long enough for the change to take effect and short enough to still attribute it.
Report progress and return as two separate figures. Progress is observed and reliable; return is an estimate built on assumptions, and merging them lends the estimate unearned credibility.
Write down the assumptions behind any time-saved-to-money conversion. Most disputed ROI claims fail on the conversion rather than on the measurement.

name: Inner / Outer Loop Time Spent
alsoknownas: Time Spent in Different Applications/Activities; Time Spent in Value-added Activities
description:
The proportion of a developer's working time spent on inner-loop activities (coding, building, unit testing) vs. outer-loop activities (integration testing, releasing, deployment). Typically collected via self-report survey or time-tracking tools.
Software development activities can be arranged in two loops. The inner loop covers activities directly related to creating the product: coding, building, and unit testing. The outer loop covers tasks needed to push code to production: integration testing, releasing, and deployment. Maximizing inner-loop time is desirable — it directly generates value and is what most developers find most engaging. Better tooling and automation for outer-loop activities frees up more time for inner-loop work.

implementation.target_goal: 60% or more of development time in the inner loop
recipe_steps: Publish the classification before measuring: which activities count as inner loop and which as outer. Disagreement about where integration testing or code review belongs is the main source of noise in this metric.
Prefer a periodic self-report over continuous time tracking. For a small team the survey is cheaper, far less intrusive, and accurate enough to act on.
Ask about a specific recent week rather than a typical week. Typical-week estimates drift towards what people think the answer should be.
State that the figure is approximate when reporting it. Self-reported time allocation is reliable for trends and direction, not for precise percentages.
Act by automating the single largest outer-loop activity. That is the whole point of the metric: outer-loop time is the part tooling can remove.

name: Number of Interruptions
alsoknownas: Nature of Interruptions
description: Measures the number of interruptions.

implementation.cadence: Weekly, during a one or two week sampling period
implementation.target_goal: Fewer than 5 unplanned interruptions per developer per day
recipe_steps: Define an interruption explicitly: unplanned, requiring an immediate context switch, and breaking focused work. Without a definition, people count very different things.
Sample over one or two weeks rather than measuring continuously. Asking developers to tally interruptions permanently is itself an interruption, and the data quality falls off quickly.
Record the source of each interruption: a colleague, an alert, an unplanned meeting, or a production issue. The source determines the remedy and the raw count does not.
Read it alongside Focus Time. The two describe the same problem from different directions, and acting on one without the other usually fails.
Address the single dominant source rather than the total. Interruptions are rarely evenly distributed, and one alerting channel or one recurring question often accounts for most of them.

name: Change Lead Time
alsoknownas: Deployment Time; Lead Time for Changes; Lead time; Time from Commit to Deploy
description: This metric measures the time it takes for a code commit or change to be successfully deployed to production. It reflects the efficiency of your software delivery process to deliver value to customers.

implementation.target_goal: Under 1 day for the DORA elite band; under 1 week for the high band
recipe_steps: Use the DORA definition: first commit of a change to that change running in production. If you also track Cycle Time, agree in writing how the two differ or they will be reported interchangeably.
Capture the commit SHA in deployment metadata so commits and deployments can be joined automatically.
Report the median per week, and the 85th percentile alongside it to expose the slow tail.
Split by change type. Hotfixes travel fast by design and will flatter the overall figure.
Compare against the DORA bands rather than an internally invented target.

name: Line Coverage
alsoknownas: Code Coverage
description: Line Coverage is a code coverage metric that measures the percentage of lines in a codebase that have been executed during testing. It helps determine how well a test suite exercises the code.

implementation.cadence: Per pull request, with a weekly trend review
implementation.target_goal: No decrease from the current baseline. Avoid setting an absolute percentage target
recipe_steps: Measure coverage on changed lines rather than across the whole codebase. Diff coverage is actionable at review time; total coverage moves too slowly to inform any decision.
Set a ratchet rather than a target: coverage must not fall below the current level. An absolute percentage target reliably produces tests written to execute lines without asserting anything.
State the limitation wherever the number appears. Line coverage records that a line ran during a test, not that its behaviour was checked, and fully covered code can contain no assertions at all.
Exclude generated code, migrations and vendored dependencies, which otherwise dominate the figure and move it for reasons unrelated to testing.
Never mandate a coverage percentage for individuals or teams. This is among the most reliably gamed metrics in the catalog and the gaming is hard to detect in review.

name: Linting Duration
description: The duration needed to lint apps and packages locally or in a pipeline.

implementation.target_goal: Under 10 seconds locally on changed files; under 2 minutes in the pipeline
recipe_steps: Measure local and pipeline linting separately. They have different acceptable durations and different fixes, and one combined figure obscures both.
Lint only changed files locally and the full tree in CI. Running the full lint on every local commit is the usual reason this metric gets bad.
Treat 10 seconds as the practical ceiling locally. Beyond that developers start bypassing the hook, and the metric stops describing anything real because the slow runs stop happening.
Check whether a faster linter exists for your stack before optimising configuration. Ruff for Python and Biome for JavaScript are typically an order of magnitude faster than the tools they replace.
Keep the pipeline lint as the enforcing gate and the local lint as fast feedback. Trying to make one do both jobs is what produces slow local runs.

name: Mean Time to Recover
alsoknownas: MTTR; Mean Time to Resolution; Time to Restore Services
description:
Mean Time to Recover (MTTR) is a key DevOps and IT reliability metric that measures the average time it takes to restore a system after a failure. It reflects how quickly teams can diagnose, fix, and recover from incidents.
Time from bug report to fix deployment. Shows quality response capability.

implementation.target_goal: Median under 1 hour for Sev1 and Sev2 incidents
recipe_steps: Define the clock precisely: start at detection, or at customer impact if you can establish it, and stop when service is restored rather than when the postmortem closes.
Record both timestamps in the incident tool for every incident, not just the large ones. Inconsistent logging is the usual reason this metric is unusable.
Report the median by severity. A single multi-day outage will dominate the mean and hide the normal case.
Separate time to detect from time to fix. They have completely different remedies.
Review the figure in postmortems rather than on a dashboard, where it rarely prompts action.

name: Communication Network Density
description: Network metrics that show who is connected to whom and how.

implementation.target_goal: No isolated team members and no single person brokering communication between sub-teams. No numeric target
recipe_steps: Build the graph from work artefacts, such as who reviews whose pull requests, rather than from message content. It answers the same question and is far less intrusive.

Check your legal position before collecting communication data. In much of Europe this requires works council consultation or an explicit lawful basis, and retrofitting consent after collection is not possible.
Report only at team level and never name individuals. A network graph that identifies people will be read as surveillance regardless of intent.

Look for two specific patterns rather than a density number: isolated nodes, meaning people nobody collaborates with, and single brokers connecting otherwise disconnected groups. Both are concrete risks.
Act by rotating reviewers or deliberately pairing across the gap. The structure is the finding; the density figure itself is not actionable.

name: Number of Deployments
alsoknownas: Deploy Count; Deployment Count; Total Deployments
description: Measures the number of deployments.

implementation.target_goal: No target in isolation. Use Deployment Frequency, which expresses the same data as a rate
recipe_steps: Recognise that this is a raw count of the same events Deployment Frequency measures as a rate. If you already track Deployment Frequency, this metric adds nothing and is a candidate for retirement.
If you do track it, fix the denominator you implicitly compare against: deployments per week for a team of three and a team of thirty are not comparable numbers.
Define what counts as a deployment once and apply it consistently, including whether rollbacks and configuration-only changes are counted.
Count from the deployment pipeline rather than from release tickets, which are often batched or created retrospectively.
Prefer reporting it per service or per team. An organisation-wide count is dominated by whichever service deploys most often.

name: Number of Escaped Bugs
alsoknownas: Bugs Fixed; Introduced Bugs; Number of Bugs Post Release; Number of Issues Logged; Priority Tickets/Bugs Undertaken Mid-Sprint
description: Measures the number of defects or issues that escape testing and reach production. It measures the effectiveness of testing processes and helps identify weaknesses in quality assurance.

implementation.target_goal: Under 10% of all defects discovered in production rather than before release
recipe_steps: Define an escaped bug as a defect found after release that an existing or reasonable test could have caught. Issues arising from genuinely unforeseeable conditions are a different category.
Tag defects at the point of discovery with whether they were found pre-release or in production. Reconstructing this later is unreliable.
Report the escape rate, escaped divided by total defects found, rather than the raw count. The raw count moves with release volume and will mislead.
Distinguish it from Number of Customer-Reported Defects, which counts by reporter. A bug your monitoring catches in production is escaped but not customer-reported.
For each escaped bug, record which test layer should have caught it, and add that test. The action is the point of this metric, not the trend line.

name: Number of Handoffs
alsoknownas: Handoffs
description: Measures how many times work is transferred between individuals, teams, or systems during a workflow.

implementation.cadence: Monthly, supported by an annual value stream mapping session
implementation.target_goal: Three or fewer handoffs per work item
recipe_steps: Count transitions that change the owning person or team. A status change within the same team is not a handoff and including it inflates the number.
Map one representative work item end to end by hand before automating anything. Teams routinely discover handoffs that exist in practice but not in the tracker.
Measure the wait time at each handoff, not just the count. Handoffs matter because of the queueing they create, and a count alone does not show where the time goes.
Include handoffs to groups outside engineering, such as security review, legal or procurement. These are frequently the longest waits and the easiest to overlook.
Reduce handoffs by cross-skilling or merging adjacent stages rather than by asking people to move work faster through the existing path.

name: Time for Onboarding New Hires
description: Measures the onboarding time for new members, also including HR-related onboarding.

implementation.target_goal: First independent change in production within 30 days; full ramp within 90
recipe_steps: Define the end point concretely, for example the first change the new hire ships to production without pairing. Ready is not measurable and will be interpreted differently by every manager.
Include HR and IT onboarding in the clock: laptop, accounts and repository access. Access delays are the most common cause of slow ramp-up and the easiest to fix.
Track checklist completion alongside elapsed time. A fast ramp with half the checklist skipped is storing up problems.
Review per cohort rather than per individual. Individual ramp speed varies for many legitimate reasons and is not a performance signal.
Keep this distinct from Experience of New Members, which captures how onboarding felt. This metric measures elapsed time; that one measures whether the time was well spent.

name: Operational Activity
description: Refers to the routine tasks and processes required to maintain, monitor, and support software systems in production. These activities ensure the system remains stable, secure, and performant while minimizing downtime.

implementation.target_goal: Under 20% of team capacity spent on unplanned operational work
telemetry_sources: Jira with an operational work label
recipe_steps: Separate scheduled maintenance from unplanned, interrupt-driven work. They have different causes and only the second one damages focus.
Label operational work at intake. Retrospective classification consistently undercounts the small interruptions that make up most of the load.
Express the result as a share of team capacity rather than in absolute hours, so it remains comparable as the team changes size.
Report who carries the load. Operational work concentrates on a few people, and a team average will hide someone spending half their time on it.
Automate the single most frequent recurring task each quarter. Operational load is dominated by repetition, and one automation usually removes a disproportionate share.

name: Service Readiness Score
alsoknownas: Service Operational Readiness Score
description: A composite score assessing how well individual services meet operational standards (e.g., monitoring/alarm coverage, runbook completeness, on-call readiness, error-budget adherence) used to track production maturity across a microservices portfolio.

implementation.target_goal: Every production service meeting the agreed minimum checklist before it is considered production-ready
recipe_steps: Define the checklist explicitly: monitoring coverage, alerting with a named owner, a current runbook, on-call rotation, and documented dependencies. Vague readiness cannot be scored.
Score each item as met or not met rather than on a scale. Binary items avoid arguments about weighting and are far cheaper to assess honestly.
Automate what you can read from configuration, such as whether alerts exist and whether a runbook link is present in the service catalog.
Publish per service and never as a portfolio average. One unready service is a risk that an average will conceal.
Gate new services on a minimum score at launch. Retrofitting operational readiness after a service is live is substantially more expensive.

name: Operational Health and Security Score
description: Tracks the operational health and security posture of production systems. As currently defined, this metric is vague and underspecified as it doesn't specify which signals are tracked or how they're aggregated.

implementation.target_goal: No critical vulnerabilities older than 7 days and no service below the agreed minimum
recipe_steps: Start by specifying what the score actually covers. The catalog definition notes this metric is underspecified, so the first task is choosing which signals you aggregate: patch currency, open vulnerabilities, monitoring coverage, incident frequency, or some subset.
Keep the security and reliability components separate rather than merging them into one figure. They have different owners, different urgency and different remedies.
Report the age of the oldest unresolved critical finding rather than a count. One critical vulnerability open for three months is worse than twenty opened yesterday, and a count cannot express that.
Automate dependency and image scanning so the data is collected continuously rather than assembled by hand before each review.
Never let a composite score average away a critical finding. Set a rule that any open critical issue caps the score regardless of the other components.

name: Perceived Productivity
alsoknownas: Self-reported Productivity
description: The self-reported productivity by an individual (might be aggregated on team level).

implementation.target_goal: 4.0 or higher on a 5-point scale
recipe_steps: Anchor the question to a defined recent period, for example the past two weeks. Unanchored questions measure mood rather than anything about the work.
Add one open text question asking what got in the way. The rating tells you whether to look; the text tells you where.
Aggregate to team level only and state that individual responses are never reported. Self-reported productivity attributed to individuals will not be answered honestly.
Compare it against your objective delivery metrics. Where perceived productivity falls while throughput holds steady, the gap is the finding and usually points at friction rather than output.
Expect perception and measured output to diverge, particularly where AI tooling is in use. Treat the divergence as information rather than as an error in one of the two measures.

name: Perceived Rate of Delivery
description: A subjective metric that reflects how fast stakeholders (e.g., customers, executives, or internal teams) believe software is being delivered, regardless of the actual speed. It’s influenced by communication, transparency, and user experience rather than just raw deployment frequency.

implementation.target_goal: 4.0 or higher on a 5-point scale from stakeholders outside the engineering team
recipe_steps: Survey stakeholders rather than engineers. This metric is specifically about external perception, and asking the delivery team measures something else entirely.
Run it in the same quarter you measure actual deployment frequency or cycle time, so the two can be compared directly.
Treat the gap between perceived and actual delivery speed as the primary finding. A team delivering quickly but perceived as slow has a communication problem, not a delivery problem.
Segment by stakeholder group. Sales, support and executives form their impressions from different evidence and will diverge.
Act on transparency first, through roadmap visibility and release communication, before acting on delivery speed. Perception usually responds faster to the former.

name: Perceived Software Quality
description: Evaluates how users perceive the overall quality of a software product. This metric is subjective and focuses on user satisfaction, usability, and the software’s ability to meet user expectations. It often involves collecting feedback through surveys, such as Customer Satisfaction (CSAT) scores, which measure user perceptions of quality based on their experience with the product.

implementation.target_goal: 4.0 or higher on a 5-point scale
recipe_steps: Ask users rather than the development team. Internal estimates of perceived quality are consistently wrong in both directions.
Distinguish it from Customer Satisfaction Score, which covers the whole relationship including support, pricing and onboarding. This metric is about the software itself.
Ask about reliability, usability and performance as separate items. They fail independently and a single quality rating cannot be acted on.
Compare against your objective error rates and defect counts. Where perception is worse than the measured data, the problem is usually in a small number of highly visible flows.
Route verbatims to the owning team by component. The comments identify which part of the product is driving the perception.

name: Regrettable Attrition Rate
alsoknownas: Percentage of Regrettable Attrition
description: Refers to the voluntary departure of highly valued employees whose loss significantly impacts the organization.

implementation.target_goal: Under 5% annualised. For teams under about 20 people, report the count rather than a percentage
recipe_steps: Write down the rule for what counts as regrettable before anyone leaves. Classifying departures after the fact is unavoidably biased and will not survive scrutiny.
Use a rolling 12-month window. Quarterly attrition in a small organisation is dominated by single events and the percentage will swing wildly.
For small teams, report the absolute count instead of a rate. One departure from a team of eight is 12.5%, which reads as a crisis and usually is not.
Read it alongside engagement and burnout indicators from previous quarters. Attrition is a lagging measure, and its value lies in validating whichever leading signal you already collect.
Keep individual reasons confidential and report only themes. Exit interview candour depends entirely on this, and one breach ends it permanently.

name: Percentage of Time Spent on New Capabilities
alsoknownas: Innovation rate
description: Measures the proportion of a team's time dedicated to building new features or capabilities, as opposed to activities like maintenance, bug fixes, or refactoring.

implementation.target_goal: 60 to 70% of effort on new capabilities; set the split locally with product
telemetry_sources: Jira with a work type label
recipe_steps: Define the categories before measuring: new capability, maintenance, defect fix, operational toil and technical debt. Ambiguous categories are the main source of error here.
Label work at intake rather than reconstructing it at month end. Retrospective labelling systematically overstates the new capability share.
If time tracking is too heavy, weight issue counts by estimate instead. An approximate split from existing data beats an accurate one nobody maintains.
Report the trend across several months. A single month is dominated by whatever large item happened to land in it.
Treat a very high new capability share as a warning rather than a success. Sustained above roughly 80% usually means maintenance and debt are being deferred rather than avoided.

name: Pull Request Cycle Time
description: Measures the total time a pull request spends in all stages of the development pipeline, from the first commit to when the pull request is merged into the codebase (e.g. to the main/production branch). It provides insights into the efficiency of the code review and merging process, helping teams identify bottlenecks and improve workflows.

implementation.target_goal: Median under 24 hours from first commit to merge
recipe_steps: Define it as first commit to merge. Cycle Time and Change Lead Time extend to production, and the three are routinely confused when reported side by side.
Break the total into authoring, waiting for pickup, active review, rework and waiting to merge. The breakdown is what you act on.
Expect pickup wait to be the largest sub-stage in most teams. It is also the cheapest to fix, usually through a review rota rather than through tooling.
Report the median with the 85th percentile. A few long-running pull requests will distort any mean and those are exactly the ones causing frustration.
Segment by pull request size before drawing conclusions. Large changes legitimately take longer, and mixing them with small ones makes the metric look worse than the process is.

name: Post-Submission Edit Ratio
alsoknownas: Edit Ratio; Pull Request Maturity; Total Number of Changelists
description: The percentage of code changes within a pull request that occur after it has been submitted for review. Aims to minimize back-and-forth during review, enabling quicker, more decisive reviews and faster integration.

implementation.target_goal: Under 30% of a pull request's lines changed after it was opened for review
recipe_steps: Calculate the share of lines changed in commits made after the pull request was opened, relative to the total lines in the merged change.
Exclude merge commits, rebases and formatting-only commits, which otherwise dominate the ratio without representing real rework.
Read a high ratio as design happening during review rather than before it. The fix is earlier discussion, not faster reviewers.
Pair it with Pull Request Size. Large pull requests reliably produce more post-submission editing, and the size is usually the easier thing to change.
Encourage draft pull requests for work in progress so exploratory commits do not count against the ratio and reviewers are not pulled in early.

name: Pull Request Size
alsoknownas: PR Size
description: An indicator of overall code review efficiency. Small PRs mean faster pickup time, reviews, and cycles–translating to faster time to value. Larger PRs often result in fewer meaningful comments. For example, PRs with more than 250 lines of code could be tagged.

implementation.target_goal: Median under 250 lines changed, with fewer than 10% of pull requests exceeding 400
recipe_steps: Count lines added plus deleted, excluding generated files, lockfiles and vendored dependencies. Without those exclusions the metric measures dependency updates.
Report the share of pull requests above your threshold alongside the median. The share is more actionable, because the problem is the tail rather than the typical case.
Use the threshold as a review signal rather than a block. Some changes genuinely cannot be split, and a hard limit encourages artificial splitting that is worse for reviewers.
Read it next to Pull Request Cycle Time and Quality of Code Reviews. Large pull requests predictably produce slower reviews and fewer substantive comments.
Act at planning time by breaking work into smaller deliverable units. Asking developers to split a finished change at review time wastes the work already done.

name: Custom Quality Metric
alsoknownas: Code Maintainability; Code Quality; Process Quality; System Quality; Unit Test Quality
description: Relates to code reliability, maintainability, and alignment with user/business outcomes. It may be measured through metrics that assess both technical rigor and real-world impact, emphasizing sustainable practices over superficial outputs. Usually highly company-specific implementation.

implementation.cadence: Define once, then review monthly and redefine each quarter
implementation.target_goal: Set locally when the metric is defined. There is no transferable target for this metric
recipe_steps: Run a short workshop to agree what quality means for this codebase and this product. This metric is company-specific by definition and cannot be adopted off the shelf.
Pick two or three observable signals that stand in for that definition, for example escaped defects, change failure rate or a maintainability index.
Write down what each signal does not capture, so the gap is explicit rather than discovered later.
Establish a baseline over four weeks before setting any target.
Revisit the definition each quarter. A custom quality metric that outlives the problem it was created for is the clearest candidate for retirement.

name: Quality of Documentation
alsoknownas: Self-Service Documentation; Written Communication Effectiveness Through Design Documents
description: Measures how well documentation supports the software development process, particularly in enabling developers to work efficiently and effectively.

implementation.target_goal: 4.0 or higher on a 5-point scale for whether documentation let the reader finish the task without asking someone
telemetry_sources: Confluence or Notion page feedback widget
recipe_steps: Ask a task-oriented question rather than asking people to rate the documentation. Whether someone completed their task without asking a colleague is answerable; overall quality is not.
Add an inline feedback control to documentation pages so ratings attach to specific pages rather than to the corpus as a whole.
Keep this distinct from Discoverability of Documentation and Expertise. That metric asks whether people can find the page; this one asks whether the page helped once found.
Cross-reference page traffic with page rating. High traffic and low rating is your prioritised rewrite list, and it is usually short.
Put a review-by date on the pages that matter most. Documentation quality decays silently, and nothing in the measurement will tell you a page went stale.

name: Quality of Code Reviews
description: Measures quality of code reviews contributed by team members.

implementation.cadence: Quarterly for the survey, with monthly sampling
implementation.target_goal: 4.0 or higher on a 5-point scale from pull request authors on whether reviews improved their change
telemetry_sources: Sampled manual assessment against a rubric
recipe_steps: Ask authors whether the review improved their change. They are the only people positioned to judge whether a review was useful, and the question is specific enough to answer honestly.
Supplement with a monthly sample of ten reviews read against a short rubric: did it catch defects, did it question design, was it timely, was the tone constructive.
Do not use comment count as a quality proxy. It rewards nitpicking and penalises the reviewer who spots the one structural problem and says so in a sentence.
Track the share of pull requests approved with no comments at all as a separate warning signal. A high rate usually means rubber-stamping rather than flawless code.
Read it alongside Pull Request Size. Review quality falls sharply above a few hundred lines, and the size is usually the easier thing to fix.

name: R&D as Percentage of Revenue
description: Measures how much of a company’s total revenue is invested in research and development (R&D).

implementation.target_goal: No engineering target. Benchmarks vary widely by company stage and sector and are not comparable across them
recipe_steps: Take the figure from finance rather than reconstructing it from engineering data. Engineering does not own this metric and a parallel calculation will not match the official one.
Agree what is included in R&D and keep the definition stable: whether operations, quality assurance, product management and infrastructure count materially changes the result.
Compare only against your own history or against companies at the same stage and in the same sector. A published industry average spanning seed startups and listed enterprises means nothing.
Treat this as a board-level allocation metric rather than a measure of engineering performance. Nothing an engineering team does in a quarter should be judged by it.
Do not use it on its own to argue for headcount. The argument needs a capability or delivery case, and the ratio alone will not carry it.

name: Release Frequency
alsoknownas: Release Count
description: How often features reach users (independent of deployment frequency, such as when feature flags or staged rollouts are used).

implementation.target_goal: Set locally. The right frequency depends on your product and release model, not on an industry figure
recipe_steps: Measure when a feature becomes available to users, not when the code deploys. The catalog definition is explicit on this point and the two diverge sharply once feature flags are in use.
Where you use flags, treat flag enablement as the release event and record it. Deployment pipelines will not show you this.
Track staged rollouts by exposure percentage rather than as a single release event, so a feature at 5% of users is not counted the same as one at 100%.
Keep this distinct from Deployment Frequency. A team can deploy daily and release monthly, and conflating the two hides exactly that pattern.
Read it next to Time to Market for New Features. Release frequency tells you the cadence; time to market tells you whether the cadence is translating into value reaching users.

name: Reliability Score
alsoknownas: Availability; Latency; Performance; Scalability
description: A composite reliability measure covering availability (uptime %), latency (response time percentiles), performance, and scalability (behavior under load). DORA's original 2021 methodology measured this via self-rated survey ('are you meeting your reliability targets?'), but the underlying components can also be tracked quantitatively via system telemetry.

implementation.cadence: Quarterly for the survey component, continuously for telemetry
implementation.target_goal: Meeting your own stated reliability targets. The score is meaningless without those targets defined first
recipe_steps: Define service level objectives before measuring anything. The original DORA question asks whether you are meeting your reliability targets, which cannot be answered if no targets exist.
Measure the components separately: availability, latency percentiles, error rate and behaviour under load. They fail independently and a single score cannot direct any action.

State which method you are using. The DORA original is a self-rated survey, while the same dimensions can be measured from telemetry, and the two produce different numbers that are not interchangeable.
Report error budget consumption as the headline figure. It is the single most actionable number in this area because it translates directly into whether to ship or to stabilise.
