Always display the components alongside any composite. As with other composite scores, if nobody drills into the components within two quarters, retire the composite.

name: Response Time
description: Measures the server’s speed in fulfilling user requests.

implementation.target_goal: 95th percentile under 500ms for interactive endpoints; set separate targets per endpoint class
recipe_steps: Report percentiles, never averages. A mean response time is dominated by the fast majority and will look healthy while a meaningful share of users wait seconds.
Set targets per endpoint class. A search endpoint, a write operation and a static asset have different reasonable expectations and one global threshold serves none of them.
Measure server-side and client-perceived timing separately. Users experience network, rendering and server time together, and server-side numbers alone will look better than reality.
Exclude health checks, synthetic monitors and known bot traffic, which are fast and numerous enough to pull the percentiles down.
Alert on regression against a rolling baseline rather than on a fixed threshold. Gradual degradation is the common failure mode and a static threshold will not catch it until it is severe.

name: Employee Retention Rate
alsoknownas: Employment Retention
description: How well an organization retains its employees over a given period.

implementation.target_goal: 90% or higher annualised. Below about 20 people, report headcount changes rather than a rate
recipe_steps: Define the population and the window explicitly, including how joiners partway through the period are counted. Different conventions produce materially different rates.
Track either retention or attrition, not both. They are complements, and reporting both invites arithmetic disputes that distract from the finding.
For small teams, report the absolute numbers. A rate calculated over eight people swings by double digits on a single departure and will be over-interpreted.
Segment by tenure band. First-year departures usually indicate hiring or onboarding problems, while departures after three years usually indicate progression problems, and the aggregate hides both.
Read it alongside Regrettable Attrition Rate. Overall retention can look healthy while the people you most wanted to keep are the ones leaving.

name: Revenue Growth Rate
description: Measures the growth of revenue, such as year over year.

implementation.target_goal: No engineering target. This is a company metric reported for context, not an engineering objective
recipe_steps: Take this from finance and report it unchanged. Engineering has no independent means of calculating revenue and should not attempt one.

Include it only as context alongside engineering metrics, never as an engineering key result. Revenue responds to pricing, sales, market conditions and product decisions that engineering does not control.
Resist drawing causal links between engineering activity and revenue movement in the same period. The lag is long and variable, and the attribution will not survive challenge.
If you want a traceable link between engineering work and business outcomes, use Business Objective Advancement or Initiative Progress and ROI, which are designed for it.
Agree with the business which revenue figure is used, such as recognised, booked or annual recurring, and keep it consistent across reports.

name: Revenue per Engineer
description: Measures the average revenue per engineer.

implementation.target_goal: No target. Treat as context only, and never as an efficiency measure for engineering
recipe_steps: Understand what the ratio does before reporting it. Revenue divided by engineering headcount improves when revenue rises for reasons unrelated to engineering, and it also improves when you make engineers redundant.
Never use it as an efficiency target. It is one of the few metrics in this catalog that can be improved by actively harming the organisation's capability.
Define the denominator explicitly: engineers only, or the whole product organisation including design, product management and quality assurance. The two produce very different figures.
Compare only against your own history and only over multiple years. Period-to-period movement is dominated by hiring timing and revenue recognition.
If the question behind this metric is whether engineering investment is paying off, use Initiative Progress and ROI instead, which can actually be traced to decisions.

name: Dependency Update Automation Rate
alsoknownas: Self-Serve Dependency Maintenance
description: The share of dependency updates (internal services and third-party/open-source libraries) that are applied automatically without requiring manual developer intervention. Used as a proxy for how much interrupt-driven toil developers face for keeping their stack current. Measured via developer survey.

implementation.target_goal: 80% or more of dependency updates merged without manual intervention
recipe_steps: Measure this from pull request data rather than by survey. The catalog describes a survey-based method, but automatically merged bot pull requests divided by total bot pull requests is cheaper, continuous and more reliable. State which method you used.
Require passing CI before any automatic merge. Automation without a gate converts a toil problem into a reliability problem.
Separate patch and minor updates, which are generally safe to automate, from major version bumps, which should not be. Reporting them together hides whether the automation is actually safe.
Track the age of your oldest outdated dependency as a companion figure. A high automation rate is compatible with a handful of ancient, pinned dependencies nobody dares touch.
Review which updates consistently fail automation. The recurring failures identify the fragile parts of your test suite more reliably than most quality metrics.

name: Tool Sentiment Score
description: Developers' emotional responses and perceptions of their interactions with tools, documentation, and workflows. It focuses on how developers feel about using the platform and whether they find it empowering, frustrating, or aligned with their goals.

implementation.target_goal: 4.0 or higher on a 5-point scale for each tool individually
recipe_steps: Ask about each tool separately rather than about tooling in general. An overall score averages away the one tool everybody dislikes, which is the only actionable finding in the data.
Keep the list to five to eight tools. Longer lists lower the response rate and produce ratings from people who barely use half of them.
Include a direct question on whether the respondent would keep the tool. It is more decisive than a satisfaction rating and maps onto an actual decision.
Keep it distinct from Developer Satisfaction, which covers the development experience as a whole. This metric is specifically about individual tools.
Feed the results into renewal and procurement decisions. That is the action this metric exists to support, and without it the survey is just a complaint channel.

name: Speed
description: Relates to how quickly software engineers can accomplish their tasks, focusing on the efficiency of workflows and processes that enable rapid delivery without compromising quality. This includes quantiative metrics (logs for task durations, deployment statistics, and CI/CD pipeline metrics) and qualitative metrics (developer surveys, diary studies, and interviews to understand perceptions and identify pain points).

implementation.target_goal: No target for the umbrella. Set targets on the underlying measures instead
recipe_steps: Recognise this as an umbrella over measures you may already track. If you collect Cycle Time, Change Lead Time or Pull Request Cycle Time, you are already measuring most of what this covers.
Adopt it only if you specifically want a paired view: one objective duration measure and one perceived speed measure, read together.
Pair exactly one quantitative measure with one survey question rather than assembling several of each. The value is in the comparison, not in coverage.
Treat the gap between measured and perceived speed as the finding. Where the data says fast and developers say slow, the friction is usually in waiting rather than in working.
Do not report this as a single composite number. Combining durations and survey responses into one score produces a figure that cannot be interpreted or acted on.

name: Velocity
alsoknownas: Developer Velocity; Sprint Velocity
description: The amount of work completed per sprint/time period. Helps with planning and tracking.

implementation.target_goal: Predictability, not growth. A stable velocity with a narrow range is the goal
recipe_steps: Use this for forecasting only. Velocity was designed to help a team predict what it can take on, and it does that job well and almost no other job at all.
Never compare velocity between teams. Story points are calibrated within a team by construction, and cross-team comparison is meaningless regardless of how the points were agreed.
Never set velocity as a target. Points inflate immediately and silently once anyone is measured on them, and the estimation signal is then lost permanently.
Report a rolling three-sprint average with the range rather than a single sprint figure. The range is what tells you whether the forecast is trustworthy.
If you find velocity being used in performance discussions, retire it. A compromised estimation scale is worse than no velocity measure, because planning silently degrades.

name: Service Uptime Percentage
alsoknownas: Availability; Production Downtime; Production Incidents; Stability; Stability of Apps; Stability of Services; System Uptime
description: Measures the percentage of time services and apps are available/operational, and the rate of production incidents (outages, change failures, time-to-recovery): the system's track record of staying up and recovering quickly. An improved rate reduces time teams spend addressing bugs and outages, increasing operational efficiency.

implementation.target_goal: 99.9% for user-facing services, which allows roughly 43 minutes of downtime per month. Set per service
recipe_steps: Measure availability from outside your infrastructure using synthetic checks. Internal health checks routinely report a service as up while users cannot reach it.
Set targets per service rather than one organisation-wide figure. An internal admin tool and a customer-facing API do not warrant the same target or the same cost.
Express the result as error budget consumed rather than as a percentage. Saying nineteen of your forty-three allowed minutes are gone prompts a decision; saying 99.96% does not.

Decide explicitly whether planned maintenance is excluded, and make it match whatever your customer agreements say. Excluding it internally while counting it externally produces uncomfortable surprises.
Translate the target into minutes when communicating it. Most people cannot intuitively convert 99.9% into downtime, and the minutes make the trade-off concrete.

name: Talent Capability Score
description: Evaluates the alignment of workforce skills with technical/domain/operational needs; identifies gaps constraining delivery or innovation.

implementation.cadence: Semi-annually, and whenever the technical roadmap changes materially
implementation.target_goal: No critical capability dependent on a single person
recipe_steps: Build the matrix from the capabilities your roadmap actually requires over the next year, not from a generic industry skills list. A generic list produces gaps nobody needs to close.
Combine self-assessment with manager calibration. Self-assessment alone is unreliable in both directions and calibration alone misses capability people have but do not use.
Look for coverage gaps and single points of failure rather than computing an average score. One person holding a critical capability is the finding worth acting on.
Never use this for individual performance assessment. The moment it affects reviews, self-assessments become strategic and the matrix stops describing reality.
Refresh it when the roadmap changes rather than on a fixed calendar. Skills requirements move with technical direction, not with the financial year.

name: Upskilling Rate
alsoknownas: Skill development; Technical expertise development
description: Measures the rate/volume of upskilling and cross-training activity (e.g., courses completed, certifications, AI-accelerated learning) within the organization.

implementation.target_goal: Set locally against identified capability gaps. A volume target produces activity rather than capability
recipe_steps: Pair this with Talent Capability Score. Counting courses measures activity, and only the capability picture tells you whether the activity closed anything.
Count completion rather than enrolment. Enrolment numbers are easy to grow and tell you nothing about whether learning happened.
Include informal learning such as pairing, internal talks and documented self-study. Measuring only purchasable training will quietly bias investment towards vendors.
Relate each activity to an identified gap. Training unconnected to a known gap may still be worthwhile, but it should not count towards closing one.

Watch for the metric becoming a compliance exercise. A rising completion rate with a static capability picture means people are clicking through courses, and the metric should then be retired or redesigned.

name: Task Completion Rate
alsoknownas: Average Number of UFPs Completed; Completed Goals to Planned Goals Ratio; Completion Percentage / Completion Time; Function Points; Function Points per Month; Number of Requirements Met; Product Delivery Rate; Sprint Burndown Rates; Story Points Completed; Story Points per Sprnt; Task Completion Rate
description: Measures the rate of work completion — the volume of task units (e.g., story points, function points, requirements) completed per individual or team, typically tracked per sprint or time period, and optionally expressed as a percentage of planned work completed.

implementation.cadence: Per sprint or per two-week period
implementation.target_goal: 80 to 90% of committed work completed. Consistently hitting 100% suggests under-committing
recipe_steps: Choose one unit: story points, issues or requirements. Points are the most gameable, so issues are usually the safer choice for a small team.
Snapshot the committed scope at sprint start. Without a snapshot, scope added mid-sprint makes the figure meaningless.
Count completed items against that snapshot at sprint end, and record items added after the snapshot separately.
Review carry-over reasons in the retro rather than the percentage itself. The reasons are the actionable part.
Do not drive this towards 100%. A team that always completes everything is committing to less than it could.

name: Team Collaboration Effectiveness
alsoknownas: Communication Responsiveness; Cross-team Contribution Rate
description: Assesses how well a team communicates and coordinates, typically via signals such as code review turnaround, cross-team contribution patterns, response/communication latency, or async documentation practices — often supplemented by self-reported survey scores rather than a single quantitative figure.

implementation.target_goal: Set locally. Report the underlying signals rather than targeting a combined score
recipe_steps: Pick two or three signals you already collect, such as review turnaround, cross-team contribution and documentation practice, and add one survey item. Do not introduce new collection for this metric.
Report the signals side by side rather than combining them into a single effectiveness score. A composite here averages away the one thing that is going wrong.
If you use communication platform data, check your legal position first. In much of Europe this requires works council consultation or a documented lawful basis.
Look for structural patterns rather than levels: teams that never contribute to each other, or one person through whom all cross-team work flows.
Act on the structure through reviewer rotation, shared ownership or deliberate pairing. The survey item tells you whether the structural change was felt.

name: Technical Debt Ratio
alsoknownas: Technical Debt; Time Spent Remediating Tech Debt
description: Is an estimate of maintenance burden in codebase. It essentially compares the cost of fixing existing technical debt to the total cost of developing the software.

implementation.target_goal: Under 5%, which corresponds to the conventional A rating in most analysis tools
recipe_steps: Understand what the tool is calculating before reporting it. The ratio is estimated remediation effort divided by estimated development effort, both derived from rule violations and assumed minutes per fix. It is a model, not a measurement.
Do not compare the absolute value across tools or across languages. Different rule sets and different remediation assumptions produce different ratios for identical code.
Track the trend rather than the absolute figure. Direction is meaningful even though the level is tool-dependent.
Exclude generated code, migrations and vendored dependencies, which can dominate the estimate without representing debt anyone will ever pay down.
Read it alongside change frequency. Debt in code nobody touches costs nothing; debt in your most-modified files is what actually slows delivery.

name: Test Coverage
alsoknownas: Code Coverage Percent
description: The percentage of code covered by automated tests. Shows confidence in change safety.

implementation.cadence: Per pull request, with a weekly trend review
implementation.target_goal: No decrease from the current baseline. Avoid an absolute percentage target
recipe_steps: State which coverage type you mean: line, branch or statement. They differ substantially, and branch coverage is considerably more informative than line coverage for the same effort.
Check whether this duplicates Line Coverage in your catalog. If you already track that one, this metric only adds value when you upgrade to branch coverage.
Measure coverage on changed lines rather than across the whole codebase. Diff coverage is actionable at review time; total coverage moves too slowly to inform anything.
Set a ratchet rather than a target. An absolute percentage reliably produces tests that execute code without asserting anything about it.
Never mandate a coverage figure for individuals or teams. This is among the most reliably gamed metrics available and the gaming is difficult to spot in review.

name: Test Runner Duration
description: Measures the duration to run tests for various apps and packages locally.

implementation.target_goal: Local unit suite under 60 seconds; full suite under 10 minutes in the pipeline
recipe_steps: Measure the suite developers actually run before pushing separately from the full pipeline suite. They have different acceptable durations and different fixes.
Report the ten slowest tests rather than the total. Test time is heavily concentrated, and a handful of tests usually account for most of the wall clock.
Treat roughly two minutes as the practical ceiling for the local suite. Beyond that developers stop running it before pushing, and the fast feedback loop is lost regardless of what the metric says.
Separate slow integration tests into their own suite so the fast loop stays fast, and run the slow suite in the pipeline only.
Shard or parallelise before optimising individual tests. Parallelisation usually buys more time for less effort than rewriting assertions.

name: Value-Added Time vs. Wait Time
alsoknownas: Value-Added Time; Wait Time
description: Per the SPACE framework, decomposes the time work spends in a system into value-added time (actively being worked on) and wait time (idle — in queues, blocked, or awaiting handoff), distinguishing productive flow from delay.

implementation.target_goal: 40% or more of elapsed time spent in value-added states
recipe_steps: Classify every workflow state as either active work or waiting, and publish the classification. Ambiguous states such as in review need an explicit decision.
Derive the split from status transition timestamps rather than asking people to estimate. The tracker already holds the data.
Expect waiting to dominate, typically between 60 and 80% of elapsed time. A low value-added share is normal and is the point of measuring it.
Attack the single largest queue rather than trying to speed up active work. Active work is rarely where the time goes.
Treat this as the diagnostic behind Cycle Time. Cycle time tells you delivery is slow; this metric tells you where the time is actually sitting.

name: Time Spent in Code Review
alsoknownas: Code Review Time; Median Wall-Clock Merge Time; Median Wall-Clock Review Time; PR Time in Review; Review Time
description: Measures the time developers spend reviewing others’ code.

implementation.target_goal: 10 to 15% of development time spent reviewing
recipe_steps: Keep this distinct from Code Reviewer Response Time, which measures how long an author waits. This metric measures reviewer effort, and the two can move in opposite directions.
Prefer a periodic self-report estimate over instrumentation. Measuring true active review time requires IDE telemetry that is disproportionate for most teams.
If you approximate from first-to-last comment timestamps within a review, label the figure a proxy wherever it appears. It systematically understates reading time.
Report at team level only. Review effort attributed to individuals becomes a target and the quality of reviews falls as the counts rise.
Look at how the load is distributed rather than at the average. Review effort concentrating on two or three people is the common and actionable finding.

name: Time to Market for New Features
alsoknownas: Feature Delivery Time; Time to Release
description: Measures the duration from the initial conception of a feature to its availability for end-users.

implementation.target_goal: Set locally per feature class. A single target across all feature sizes is not meaningful
recipe_steps: Define the start point explicitly: first idea, approved for build, or first commit. Teams routinely report one while believing they measure another, and the three differ by weeks.
Define the end point as availability to users rather than deployment. Where feature flags are used, these diverge substantially.
Segment by feature size or class. Mixing a two-day change with a quarter-long initiative produces a median that describes neither.
Break the elapsed time into discovery, build and release phases. The delay is frequently before any code is written, which no engineering metric will reveal.
Read it next to Release Frequency. A short time to market with infrequent releases means features wait in a queue rather than reaching users as they complete.

name: Time to Nth Pull Request
alsoknownas: Time to First Commit; Time to Xth PR; Time to Xth Pull Request; Time to technical ability to commit
description: Measures the time it takes for a new engineer to create their Nth pull request (PR) after joining a development team. For example, the time to 1st and 10th PR at Spotify.

implementation.target_goal: First pull request within 5 working days; tenth within 60 days
recipe_steps: Pick the values of N deliberately. The first pull request measures environment setup and access; the tenth measures genuine productive ramp-up. Both are useful and they measure different things.
Count from the official start date, including any delay in getting accounts and repository access. Excluding setup time hides the most fixable part of the problem.
Expect the first pull request to be trivial and treat that as intended. A documentation fix on day two is a healthy signal, not a gamed one.
Report per cohort rather than per individual. Individual ramp speed varies for legitimate reasons and is not a performance signal.
Read it alongside Experience of New Members. A fast ramp with a poor reported experience usually means the new hire was left to work it out alone.

name: Deployments per Developer
alsoknownas: Number of Deployments per Developer
description: Quantifies the amount of weekly deployments per developer.

implementation.target_goal: No target. Use Deployment Frequency, which measures the same events without a headcount denominator
recipe_steps: Recognise that this is Deployment Frequency divided by headcount. The denominator adds no information and introduces sensitivity to team size and work splitting.
Never report it per named individual. Deployments per person is trivially increased by splitting changes, and the splitting makes review and rollback harder.
If you track Deployment Frequency already, treat this as a retirement candidate. Two views of the same events double the maintenance and the opportunity for misreading.
Where you do use it, report the team figure for capacity context only, and annotate it with team size changes.
Pair it with Change Failure Rate whenever it is shown, so a rising deployment count that is degrading stability cannot be read as improvement.

name: Code Reviews per Developer
alsoknownas: Number of Comments; PR Review Comments and Requests for Changes
description: Quantifies the number of weekly code reviews per developer.

implementation.target_goal: No individual target. No reviewer carrying more than twice the team median
recipe_steps: Report the distribution across the team rather than the average. Unlike most per-developer counts, the spread here is genuinely informative because review load should be shared.
Identify reviewers carrying a disproportionate share. Concentrated review load is a bus factor risk and a common cause of slow pickup times.
Never set a per-person review target. Counting reviews rewards fast approvals, which is precisely the behaviour that makes reviews worthless.
Read it alongside Quality of Code Reviews. A rising review count with falling perceived usefulness means people are rubber-stamping to hit the number.
Rebalance through a review rota or explicit ownership rather than by asking the overloaded person to delegate. They are usually overloaded because they are the only one who knows the area.

name: Design Docs per Developer
alsoknownas: Number of Design Docs Generated per Developer
description: Quantifies the weekly number of design documents generated per engineer.

implementation.target_goal: No target. Counting documents measures activity rather than design quality
recipe_steps: Be clear about what this counts. A number of documents says nothing about whether designs were considered, discussed or followed.
Do not mandate a rate. A required documents-per-engineer figure produces perfunctory documents written to satisfy the count, which is worse than no documents.
If the underlying question is whether significant changes have a recorded design decision, measure coverage of significant changes instead. The Design metric in this catalog covers that.
Report at team level only, and only as context for a conversation about design practice.
Treat it as a retirement candidate once a coverage-based measure exists. It is an output count standing in for a quality question.

name: Throughput
alsoknownas: Delivery Throughput; Number of Changes; Weekly Number of Diffs; Weekly Number of PRs
description: Quantifies the number of features, stories, PRs / diffs, … completed per developer within a time interval (e.g. week).

implementation.cadence: Weekly, reviewed monthly with the team
implementation.target_goal: A stable or gently rising 4-week rolling average; no fixed per-developer target
recipe_steps: Choose one unit and stick to it: merged pull requests, closed issues or completed stories. Mixing units makes the trend meaningless.
Export the completed items per week from your issue tracker or VCS API.
Aggregate at team level. Do not report per-developer figures: throughput is sensitive to work splitting and will be gamed if used for individual assessment.
Plot a 4-week rolling average and annotate it with known context such as holidays, incidents and onboarding.
Pair the trend with a quality metric such as Change Failure Rate so rising throughput at the cost of stability is visible.

name: Time Loss
alsoknownas: Lost Time, Percentage Time Lost to Obstacles
description: Quantifies the percentage (or hours) of developer time lost each week to obstacles in the work environment (e.g., unclear requirements, excessive meetings, context switching, or technical debt) typically collected via self-reported survey. Often expressed as a cost (translatable into engineering-dollar terms) to make the impact tangible to business stakeholders.

implementation.target_goal: Under 15% of developer time lost to environmental obstacles
recipe_steps: Ask for hours lost in the past week against a fixed list of obstacle categories: unclear requirements, waiting on others, meetings, context switching, tooling and technical debt.
Anchor to the past week rather than a typical week. Typical-week estimates drift towards what people believe the answer should be.
Convert the result into cost using a standard internal rate. Making the loss legible in financial terms is this metric's stated purpose and the reason it reaches business stakeholders.
Report by obstacle category. The categories are the action list; the total is only what gets the conversation started.
Present the figure as a range rather than a point estimate. Self-reported time loss is approximate, and a precise-looking number will be challenged on exactly that basis.

name: Defect Resolution Time
alsoknownas: Bug Resolution Time
description: Measures the time taken to resolve a reported defect, from identification to fix.

implementation.target_goal: Median under 5 working days for non-critical defects; per-severity targets for the rest
recipe_steps: Decide whether the clock starts at report or at triage, and state which. Triage start is fairer to the team; report start is what the customer experiences. Both are defensible, mixing them is not.
Segment by severity and report each separately. A median across all severities is dominated by low-priority items that sit for months by design.
Report the median rather than the mean. A handful of long-running defects will distort any average.
Measure time spent in each state to find whether the delay is in triage, in fixing or in waiting for release. The remedies are completely different.
Exclude defects closed as will-not-fix or duplicate, which otherwise either inflate or deflate the figure depending on how quickly they are dismissed.

name: Bug Fixing Contribution Percentage
description: Quantifies the percentage of a developer's commits made on bug-fixing tasks, relative to the rest of the team.

implementation.target_goal: No individual target. Watch for sustained concentration on one or two people
recipe_steps: Note that the catalog definition compares a developer against the rest of the team, which makes it a performance metric by construction. Decide deliberately whether you want that before adopting it.
If the question is whether defect work is fairly distributed, measure the distribution across the team without naming individuals. That answers the useful version of the question.
Treat sustained concentration on one person as an ownership and knowledge risk rather than a performance observation. It usually means only one person understands that area.
Never use this in performance review. A developer who takes on unglamorous defect work will be penalised by any interpretation that favours feature commits.
Consider Percentage of Time Spent on New Capabilities instead, which answers the same underlying question at team level without comparing individuals.

name: Career Development Opportunities
description: Is a metric that shows  the availability of career advancement opportunities.

implementation.target_goal: 4.0 or higher on a 5-point scale for whether a clear path for progression exists
recipe_steps: Ask two separate questions: whether a path for progression exists and is understood, and whether the respondent believes they can realistically follow it. Clarity and credibility fail independently.
Segment by tenure and level. Progression concerns concentrate sharply at particular career points and the aggregate will hide them.
Read it alongside Regrettable Attrition Rate. Lack of progression is among the most common reasons strong engineers leave, and this is the leading indicator for it.
Review exit interview themes against the survey. Where departing people cite progression and current staff rate it highly, the survey is not being answered candidly.
Act by publishing the progression framework and worked examples. Perceived opportunity responds far more to visible criteria than to statements of intent.

name: Complexity
alsoknownas: Average Complexity per Method; Halstead Effort by Time; Weighted Methods
description: Metrics related to complexity of methods or tasks in the coding process.

implementation.target_goal: No new function exceeding a cyclomatic complexity of 10 to 15
recipe_steps: Narrow to one measure before collecting. Cyclomatic complexity per function is the usual choice; cognitive complexity is a reasonable alternative. Measuring several at once produces noise.
Gate new and changed code rather than the whole codebase. A legacy function with a complexity of 60 that nobody touches is not costing you anything this quarter.
Combine complexity with change frequency. Code that is both complex and frequently modified is where the cost actually falls, and that intersection is a short list.
Target the outliers rather than the average. An average complexity figure is stable, uninformative and cannot be acted on.
Treat a rising complexity trend in your most-changed files as the signal to schedule refactoring, and connect it to Technical Debt Ratio rather than tracking both independently.

name: Cost per Function Point
alsoknownas: Cost per FP; Investment in Progress
description: Metrics related to cost or investments.

implementation.target_goal: No target. Function point analysis is rarely justified outside fixed-price contracting
telemetry_sources: IFPUG or COSMIC function point count
recipe_steps: Establish whether you need function points at all. Counting them properly requires trained assessors and meaningful effort, and the practice has largely been abandoned outside regulated and fixed-price contexts.
If you adopt it, choose one standard, either IFPUG or COSMIC, and apply it consistently. Counts from different standards are not comparable and the difference is large.
Take the cost side from finance rather than estimating it in engineering. A locally invented cost basis will not survive comparison with the official figures.
Do not benchmark against published industry figures unless you know which counting standard produced them. Most published cost-per-function-point data is unusable for this reason.
If what you actually need is cost per unit of delivery, define a cheaper local proxy, name it clearly as a proxy, and avoid the function point apparatus entirely.

name: Test Failure Rate
description: A metric used to measure the percentage of test cases that fail during a specific testing period or for a particular software build.

implementation.target_goal: Under 5% of test cases failing per run, excluding flakes
recipe_steps: Separate genuine failures from flaky ones before reporting anything. Without that split this metric simply restates CI Determinism from the other direction.
Keep it distinct from CI Pipeline Failure Rate, which counts whole pipeline runs. This metric counts individual test cases and the two move independently.
Report per suite rather than across the whole test estate. One unstable integration suite will dominate an aggregate and mask everything else.
Investigate a persistently very low failure rate as well as a high one. Tests that never fail may be asserting too little to catch anything.
List the top failing tests each week. Failures concentrate on a small number of tests, and fixing those few resolves most of the noise.

name: DAU/WAU/MAU for AI tools
alsoknownas: % of developers using AI chat features; AI developer tool adoption; AI model usage; AI usage events; AI usage intensity; daily active AI users; monthly active AI users; weekly active AI users
description: Daily, weekly or monthly active users of deployed AI tools.

implementation.cadence: Weekly, with a monthly stickiness review
implementation.target_goal: WAU divided by MAU of 0.6 or higher among developers holding a licence
telemetry_sources: Okta or Entra ID sign-in logs
recipe_steps: Pull both assigned seats and active users. The gap between them is usually the most interesting number.
Compute daily, weekly and monthly active users against licence holders, not against all engineers.
Calculate stickiness as WAU divided by MAU to distinguish habitual use from occasional trials.
Segment by team and seniority to find where the tool has and has not landed.
Pair this with an outcome metric. Usage shows that AI is being used, not that it is helping, and reporting it alone invites the wrong conclusion.

name: AI-Assisted PR Rate
alsoknownas: Percentage of PRs assisted by AI
description: Percentage of Pull Requests assisted by AI

implementation.target_goal: No target. This measures use rather than benefit
recipe_steps: Decide how AI assistance is recorded before measuring. A pull request template checkbox or a commit trailer is the only practical method, and both depend on self-declaration.
Expect self-declaration to be unreliable, and to decline as soon as people suspect the data informs any judgement about them. State clearly that it does not.
Set no target. A higher proportion of AI-assisted pull requests is not self-evidently better, and targeting it produces declaration rather than adoption.
The useful analysis is comparative: do AI-assisted pull requests differ from others in size, review time, post-submission editing or change failure rate.
Report at team level. Individual AI usage rates have no legitimate management use and collecting them damages the honesty of the declaration.

name: AI-Written Code Share
alsoknownas: Percentage of Code written by AI
description: Percentage of code drafted or submitted by AI

implementation.target_goal: No target. A higher share is neither good nor bad on its own
recipe_steps: Distinguish code accepted at suggestion time from code still present later. These differ substantially once developers edit what they accepted, and vendors report the first.
Treat vendor-reported percentages as acceptance data rather than authorship data. They answer a different question from the one this metric asks.
If you want a defensible figure, measure survival: the share of AI-originated lines still present after 30 days. It is harder to collect and much more meaningful.
Set no target in either direction. A high share may indicate leverage or it may indicate unreviewed generated code, and the number alone cannot distinguish them.
Never report this per developer. It is among the easiest metrics in the catalog to game and among the least informative about contribution.

name: AI Suggestion Acceptance Rate
alsoknownas: Acceptance rate of AI Suggestions
description: The percentage of AI-generated code suggestions that a developer accepts and keeps in their codebase, calculated as (suggestions accepted ÷ total suggestions shown) × 100.

implementation.target_goal: No target. Typical inline completion acceptance sits around 25 to 35%, but the figure varies by language and task
recipe_steps: Understand that acceptance is not value. A suggestion accepted and then substantially rewritten counts as accepted, and a rejected suggestion may still have saved thinking time.
Track retention alongside acceptance where the tooling allows: how much accepted code survives to merge. The gap between the two is the interesting figure.
Segment by suggestion type. Inline completion, chat-generated blocks and agent edits have very different acceptance profiles and averaging them hides all three.
Treat an unusually high acceptance rate as a warning rather than a success. It can indicate uncritical acceptance, which shows up later as review burden and defects.
Report at team level only, and pair with a quality measure such as change failure rate so acceptance cannot be read as benefit on its own.

name: AI Power Users
description: Identifying power users to help exchanging best practices.

implementation.target_goal: Identify three to five people whose practice is worth spreading. This is not a score
recipe_steps: Treat this as an identification exercise rather than a measurement. The output is a short list of people, not a number on a dashboard.
Use usage data to shortlist, then confirm by conversation. High usage alone identifies enthusiasts, not necessarily people with transferable practice.
Ask the people you identify to run a short internal session or write up their workflow. Knowledge transfer is the stated purpose of this metric and it does not happen automatically.
Never publish a usage ranking. It converts a knowledge-sharing exercise into a leaderboard and changes behaviour in ways that make the data useless.
Watch for the metric becoming adoption pressure. Developers whose work genuinely benefits less from AI should not appear as a problem to be fixed.

name: Number of Unused AI Licenses
alsoknownas: Percentage of Inactive AI Licenses
description: Identifying unused AI licenses to foster adoption or save costs.

implementation.target_goal: Under 10% of purchased licences showing no activity in the past 30 days
recipe_steps: Define unused explicitly, for example no recorded activity in 30 days, and apply the same definition each month.
Ask why before reclaiming. Non-use frequently means the tool does not fit that person's work, which is a more useful finding than the licence saving.
Reassign rather than cancel where there is a waiting list. Reallocation is faster than procurement and the cost is already sunk for the term.
Review in the month before renewal rather than continuously. Licence counts are usually only adjustable at renewal, so measuring more often produces no decision.
Keep this separate from adoption metrics. An unused licence is a cost question; low adoption is a fit or enablement question, and conflating them leads to the wrong remedy.

name: AI Spend
alsoknownas: Agent hourly rate; Percentage capacity worked per AI tool
description: Costs or capacity of AI use.

implementation.target_goal: Set against budget. Track cost per active user rather than the total
recipe_steps: Include all three components: seat licences, API or token consumption, and any dedicated infrastructure. Token spend is frequently missed and is the part that grows unpredictably.
Report cost per active user alongside the total. The total rises with headcount and tells you nothing about whether spending is efficient.
Attribute spend to teams where the billing allows it. Unattributed AI spend becomes a central line item nobody owns and nobody questions.
Watch token-based costs specifically. They scale with usage rather than with seats, and an agent workflow can change the bill by an order of magnitude without any procurement decision.
Always report this next to a value or adoption measure. Spend reported alone invites either indiscriminate cutting or unchecked growth, depending on who reads it.

name: AI Product Adoption Rate
alsoknownas: Percentage of AI Adoption in Products; Percentage of Product Features Incorporating AI
description: Monitors AI being built into products, not just used by developer throughout the SLDC.

implementation.target_goal: Set per feature. Measure engagement with shipped AI features, not the number shipped
recipe_steps: Be clear that this measures AI capability in your product, used by your customers, and not AI tooling used by your developers. The two are routinely confused because the names are similar.
Measure the share of active users engaging with each AI feature, defined per feature. An aggregate across several features hides the ones nobody uses.
Count usage rather than availability. Shipping an AI feature is not adoption, and the gap between the two is often very large.
Pair with retention and satisfaction for the users who engage. Adoption without retention usually indicates novelty rather than value.
Review features with low adoption after a fair exposure period and decide explicitly whether to improve, reposition or remove them.

name: AI Time Savings
alsoknownas: Net time gain per developer
description: Estimated time savings from using AI

implementation.target_goal: No target. Report as a range and treat as directional
recipe_steps: Ask for hours saved in the past week on specific named task types rather than in general. Open-ended savings questions produce large, unverifiable numbers.
Bound the question. Offering ranges rather than a free-text hour count reduces the inflation that self-reported savings reliably produce.
Report as a range and label it self-reported wherever it appears. A precise-looking figure will be challenged on exactly that basis, and correctly so.

Do not convert this into headcount equivalents or cost savings for anyone outside engineering without stating the method and its weakness. This conversion is where AI savings claims usually fail scrutiny.
Validate against an objective measure for the same task type, such as cycle time. Where reported savings are large and measured delivery is unchanged, that gap is the finding worth discussing.

name: Change Confidence Score
alsoknownas: AI trust, AI change confidence
description: Definition: "Developers' self-reported confidence that a code change won't break production, typically gathered via survey and used alongside change failure rate as a qualitative counterbalance to quantitative reliability metrics.

implementation.target_goal: 4.0 or higher on a 5-point scale
recipe_steps: Ask at deploy time, with a single question, triggered from the pipeline or a chat prompt. Asking quarterly loses the connection to a specific change and the answers become general sentiment.
Keep it to one question answerable in a few seconds. Anything longer will be skipped and the response rate determines whether this metric is usable.

Read it against Change Failure Rate. The informative cases are high confidence followed by failure, which reveals a blind spot, and low confidence followed by success, which reveals unnecessary caution.
Segment by service. Confidence varies far more between parts of a system than between developers.
Treat consistently low confidence as a signal about test coverage, observability or rollback capability rather than about the people deploying.

name: Developer Friction Score
alsoknownas: Ease of Application Access; Ease of Tool Access
description: A self-reported rating or open-text response of the obstacles, delays, or friction developers encounter in their daily lives, e.g. from accessing tools, applicatiosn or completing workflow tasks.

implementation.target_goal: No numeric target. The list of frictions is the output
recipe_steps: Keep the open text central. The rating tells you whether things are getting worse; the text tells you what to fix, and only the second is actionable.
Distinguish it from Time Loss, which quantifies hours lost. This metric captures what the obstacles are and how severe they feel, not how much time they cost.
Categorise responses rather than averaging a score. Ten people describing the same slow environment is a different finding from ten people describing ten different problems.
Fix the top three each quarter rather than trying to move the score. The score follows the fixes.
Report back publicly on what was fixed. Friction surveys that produce no visible change see their response rate collapse within two cycles, and the metric then becomes useless.

name: Tasks assigned to AI agents
description: Number of tasks that developers assign to their AI agents.

implementation.target_goal: No target. This is adoption tracking in a fast-moving area
telemetry_sources: Jira or Linear with an agent label
recipe_steps: Define what counts as a task assigned to an agent before collecting anything. The boundary between an autocomplete suggestion, a chat request and a delegated task is not obvious and teams will classify differently.
Measure completion and rework rates alongside the count. A task assigned to an agent and then redone by hand is worse than not assigning it, and a raw count cannot show that.
Track the human review time spent on agent output. Delegation that shifts effort from writing to reviewing may not be a saving, and this is where that shows up.
Set no target. The practice is changing quickly and a target set this quarter will be measuring the wrong thing by the next.
Plan to revise the definition within two quarters. Treat the first version as provisional and say so when reporting it.

name: Degree of Self-sufficiency
description: Degree to which AI reduces context-switching and reliance on external resources.

implementation.target_goal: No target. Interpret direction alongside Code Ownership rather than maximising
recipe_steps: Ask about specific observable behaviours, such as how often the respondent left their editor to search documentation or to ask a colleague, rather than for an abstract self-sufficiency rating.
Measure before and after introducing a tool where possible. Without a baseline this metric cannot distinguish a tool effect from the team simply becoming more experienced.
Name the downside explicitly when reporting. Reduced reliance on colleagues also means reduced incidental knowledge sharing, and that cost is invisible in this metric.
Read it alongside Code Ownership. Rising self-sufficiency with falling ownership is the pattern that indicates people are shipping code they understand less well.
Do not treat an increase as automatically positive. The useful question is whether people are unblocked faster, not whether they ask fewer questions.

name: Code Ownership
description: Whether developers maintain deep understanding of and accountability for AI-assisted code.

implementation.target_goal: 4.0 or higher on a 5-point scale for whether authors can explain and modify their own merged changes
recipe_steps: Ask authors whether they could explain and safely modify their own merged change a month later. That question gets at understanding far better than asking whether they used AI.
Sample rather than surveying every change. Ten sampled changes a month gives a usable signal at a fraction of the effort.
Read a falling score alongside rising AI usage as the clearest available indicator of accumulating cognitive debt in the codebase.
Pair it with review depth. Code nobody fully understands tends to attract shallow reviews, which compounds the problem rather than catching it.

Act through an explicit team agreement on authorship: the author owns the change, must understand it before requesting review, and flags the risk level. This is more effective than any amount of measurement.

name: Ease of Code Review
alsoknownas: Ease of Peer Review
description: Perceived ease and effort to perform a Pull Request (PR).

implementation.target_goal: 4.0 or higher on a 5-point scale from reviewers
recipe_steps: Ask the reviewer immediately after review with a single question. Retrospective quarterly answers measure the worst recent experience rather than the typical one.
Distinguish it from Quality of Code Reviews, which asks authors whether the review helped them. This metric asks reviewers how hard the review was to perform.
Read it alongside Pull Request Size and Post-Submission Edit Ratio. Both predict review difficulty, and both are easier to change than reviewer stamina.
Look at the change description as a cause. Reviews are frequently hard because the author did not explain the intent, which is cheap to fix and rarely measured.
Act by changing how work is prepared and split rather than by asking reviewers to try harder. Reviewer effort is not the variable under your control.

name: Developer Experience Index
description: Proprietary composite score that aims to predict engineering effectiveness and can be linked to financial impact. It is meant to capture whether developers have the right conditions to work effectively. Built by combining self-reports on 14 dimensions, including deep work, local iteration speed, release process, and confidence in making changes.

implementation.target_goal: Improvement against your own previous assessment. Peer benchmarking requires the vendor's dataset
recipe_steps: Be clear which instrument you are running. The Developer Experience Index is a proprietary composite from DX built on fourteen dimensions, and its benchmarking value comes from their dataset rather than from the questions alone.
Do not call a self-built survey a DXI. If you build internally, choose four or five dimensions relevant to your context and name the result something else.
Run it annually. The dimensions move slowly and a shorter cadence produces survey fatigue without new information.
Use the dimension-level results rather than the headline index. The index exists to make the result communicable upward; the dimensions are what anyone can act on.
Treat any claimed link between the index and financial impact with care when reporting outside engineering. The relationship is modelled rather than measured in your own organisation.

name: Diff Risk Score
alsoknownas: PR Risk Score
description: Predicts the likelihood of a code change (diff) causing a production incident.

implementation.target_goal: No target. Use it to direct review attention rather than to gate changes
recipe_steps: Check whether you have the data before attempting this. Predicting incident likelihood from change characteristics needs a labelled history of changes and the incidents they caused, and most small organisations do not have enough incidents to support it.

Start with simple heuristics rather than a model: change size, number of files touched, test coverage of the changed lines, and how familiar the author is with that area. These capture most of the available signal.
Use the score to route review attention towards riskier changes, not to block them. A gate will be worked around and will slow everything.
Validate against actual incidents for at least a quarter before anyone relies on it. An unvalidated risk score is a source of false confidence.
Recalculate the heuristics periodically. What predicts incidents changes as the architecture and the team change.

name: Time spent Coding
alsoknownas: Active Coding Time; Coding Time; Focus Coding Time
description: The amount or proportion of a developer's working time actively spent writing or editing code, as measured by IDE telemetry. Excludes building, testing, meetings, and other non-coding activities. Helps to identify whether developers have sufficient uninterrupted time for core development work.

implementation.target_goal: No target. A low share is not a problem in itself
recipe_steps: Check whether IDE telemetry is proportionate for your team and legally permissible before collecting it. In much of Europe this requires consultation and a documented basis, and the data is intrusive by nature.
Report at team level only, and say so in advance. Individual coding-time data has no legitimate management use and its collection will change behaviour.
Resist reading a low coding share as a problem. Review, design, collaboration and investigation are also the work, and a developer coding most of the day may simply be the only one doing none of it.
Focus on the composition of the non-coding time rather than on the coding percentage. That is where the actionable finding is.
Read it alongside Focus Time. Coding time fragmented into ten-minute slices is a different situation from the same total in two long blocks.

name: Deployment Rework Rate
alsoknownas: Rework Rate
description: The ratio of deployments that are unplanned but happen as a result of an incident in production.

implementation.target_goal: Under 10% of deployments being unplanned incident responses
telemetry_sources: Deployment logs with a hotfix tag
recipe_steps: Tag unplanned deployments at deploy time with the incident they respond to. Reconstructing this afterwards from commit messages is unreliable.
Keep it distinct from Change Failure Rate. That metric counts deployments that cause failures; this one counts the additional deployments needed to recover from them.
Compare the two directly. A high rework rate with a low change failure rate means your failures take several attempts to fix, which points at observability rather than at code quality.
Count each recovery attempt separately rather than counting one incident once. The number of attempts is the information this metric adds.
Read it with Failed Deployment Recovery Time. Together they distinguish slow recoveries from repeated unsuccessful ones, which have different remedies.

name: Pickup time
alsoknownas: PR Pickup Time; Review Request Hanging Time; Time to First Review
description: The elapsed time between a pull request's creation (or move from draft to ready-for-review) and the start of the review process, i.e., the first non-author review action.

implementation.target_goal: Median under 2 business hours from ready-for-review to first review action
recipe_steps: Define the start as the move from draft to ready-for-review, not pull request creation. Drafts can sit intentionally for days and will distort the figure.
Count the first non-author review action, excluding bot comments and automated checks, which otherwise make pickup look instantaneous.
Use business hours and handle time zones explicitly. Wall clock turns every Friday evening pull request into an apparent two-day wait.
Expect this to be the largest single component of Pull Request Cycle Time in most teams. It is also typically the cheapest to improve.
Fix it with a review rota or an agreed limit on open reviews per person rather than by publishing the number. Visibility alone rarely changes pickup behaviour.

name: Planning accuracy
alsoknownas: Delivery Predictability Score; Plan vs. Actual Ratio; Sprint Commitment Accuracy
description: The ratio of planned work actually completed within a sprint or iteration, measured in story points or issue count. High values indicate reliable delivery against commitments; low values indicate scope creep or unplanned work crowding out planned scope.

implementation.target_goal: 80 to 90% of committed work completed. Consistent 100% indicates under-commitment
recipe_steps: Check whether this duplicates Task Completion Rate in your catalog. The two definitions are close enough that tracking both is usually unnecessary.
Snapshot the committed scope at iteration start. Without a snapshot, work added mid-iteration silently changes the denominator and the ratio becomes meaningless.
Record scope added after the snapshot separately rather than folding it in. That figure is what Capacity accuracy uses.
Treat consistent 100% completion as a warning. A team that always finishes everything it committed to is committing to less than it could.
Discuss the reasons for misses in the retrospective. The ratio only indicates whether to have the conversation; the reasons are what change anything.

name: Capacity accuracy
alsoknownas: Sprint Capacity Ratio; Team Capacity Accuracy; Workload Accuracy
description: The ratio of all completed work (planned plus unplanned) to the work planned for an iteration, measured in story points or issue count.

implementation.target_goal: Close to 1.0 when read together with Planning accuracy
recipe_steps: Use the same unit and the same snapshot as Planning accuracy. The two metrics are designed to be read as a pair and diverge meaninglessly if measured differently.
Interpret them together: low planning accuracy with a capacity ratio near or above one means unplanned work displaced the plan, while low values on both means the team over-committed.
Count unplanned work explicitly rather than inferring it. Items added mid-iteration need a marker at the time they are added.
Use the pair to argue for reserved capacity. A team consistently absorbing 30% unplanned work should plan for 70%, and this is the evidence for that conversation.
Do not target either ratio in isolation. Each can be improved by changing planning behaviour in ways that make the other worse.

name: Bad Developer Days
description: A composite telemetry metric counting the share of developer-days affected by friction events such as context switching, build failures, incident response, or compliance overhead.

implementation.target_goal: Under 20% of developer-days affected by friction events
recipe_steps: Define the friction events explicitly and keep the list short: build failure, incident response, a long context switch, or blocked waiting. An open-ended list makes the metric unreproducible.
Set the threshold for what makes a day bad, for example two or more events, and keep it fixed. The threshold choice matters more than the underlying data.
Expect this to be the most demanding metric in the catalog to implement. It requires joining several telemetry sources that usually do not share identifiers.
Report at team level only. A per-developer count of bad days would be both intrusive and misleading, since exposure to incidents is rarely evenly distributed.
Act on the dominant event type rather than the overall percentage. The mix of events is the finding; the headline share only tells you whether to look.
